Learning the Cost of Reliable Inference

Dimitrios Rontogiannis Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Software Systems
Kaiserslautern, Germany
{drontogi, avelasco, manuel}@mpi-sws.org    Ander Artola Velasco Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Software Systems
Kaiserslautern, Germany
{drontogi, avelasco, manuel}@mpi-sws.org    Manuel Gomez Rodriguez Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Software Systems
Kaiserslautern, Germany
{drontogi, avelasco, manuel}@mpi-sws.org
Abstract

Benchmarking and routing platforms increasingly act as intermediaries connecting large language model providers with end-users. However, providers on these platforms typically use a fixed price per token, preventing users from achieving the most competitive price for their tasks. In this work, we design a procurement platform where token prices for each task are driven by provider competition, enabling users to secure competitive pricing for guaranteed quality levels. To this end, the platform sequentially routes queries via a reverse second-price auction that incentivizes model providers to truthfully bid their best estimate of the average cost to serve a user’s query. As it routes queries, the platform learns the quality offered by each provider and progressively routes queries to the most cost-competitive provider among those meeting a desired quality threshold. To validate our design, we conduct experiments with multiple LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families on popular mathematical reasoning and question-answering benchmarks. The results show that the pricing margin of the most cost-competitive provider on our platform varies significantly—from 10%10\% to 71%71\%—depending on the task and quality threshold. This suggests a substantial inefficiency in the current fixed-price market, and it demonstrates that our platform may enable users to capture maximum savings whenever competitive market conditions permit.

1 Introduction

The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has led to a highly competitive market of online service providers offering models of varying capabilities at different prices. To help users navigate their choice of models, benchmarking and routing platforms have become popular, letting users compare model performance on well-established tasks and even automatically selecting a provider to serve their queries.11 1 See, e.g., https://artificialanalysis.ai, https://openrouter.ai, and https://thegrid.ai.

However, existing platforms do not allow users to achieve the most competitive price for their tasks. This is because providers on these platforms typically charge users a fixed price per token,22 2 https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing, https://openai.com/api/pricing/, https://www.claude.com/pricing. which fails to reflect that a provider’s cost to serve a model and the response quality the user obtains in return depend heavily on the specific task. As a concrete illustration, consider a user who wants to use an LLM to assist with medical diagnosis and can choose between two providers, each offering a different model. Suppose the providers charge $0.06\$0.06 and $0.07\$0.07 per token, while generating a token costs them $0.01\$0.01 and $0.04\$0.04, respectively. Then, if both models produce responses of similar quality and number of tokens for the user’s task, the user—acting rationally—would select the cheapest model and pay $0.06\$0.06 per token. However, if the providers competed on price for the user’s task, the user could in principle pay as little as $0.04\$0.04 per token: the first provider would lower its per-token price down to this point, since below this the second provider—which cannot profitably price below its own cost—would no longer be a competitive alternative (Milgrom and Roberts, 1982; Mahmood, 2024; Bergemann et al., 2025b).

In this work, we design a procurement platform that addresses this price inefficiency, enabling users to secure competitive pricing on their tasks for guaranteed quality levels. To this end, the platform sequentially routes queries via a reverse second-price auction that incentivizes providers to truthfully bid their best estimate of the average cost to serve a user’s query. As it routes queries, the platform learns the quality offered by each provider and progressively routes queries to the most cost-competitive provider among those meeting a desired quality threshold. More formally, we show that, with high probability, the platform routes all but a vanishing fraction of the user’s queries to the most cost-competitive provider, whose (average) pricing margin converges to the difference between the second-lowest average cost among qualified providers and its own average cost.

To validate our platform, we conduct experiments with multiple LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families on popular mathematical reasoning and question-answering benchmarks. We find that the pricing margin of the most cost-competitive provider varies significantly—from 10%10\% to 71%71\%—depending on the task and quality threshold. This suggests a substantial inefficiency in the current fixed-price market, and it demonstrates that our platform may enable users to capture maximum savings whenever competitive market conditions permit.

Further related work. Our work contributes to a rapidly growing body of literature on the economic aspects of LLMs-as-a-service (Raghavan, 2024; Mahmood, 2024; La Malfa et al., 2024; Laufer et al., 2024; Bergemann et al., 2025c; Bergemann et al., 2025b; Olmedo et al., 2026; Velasco et al., 2026b; Velasco et al., 2026c; Velasco et al., 2026a). Within this literature, the works most closely related to ours characterize how LLM providers price their models when serving users in a competitive market. Specifically, Mahmood (2024) study the price competition between providers serving models of varying quality across different tasks, while Bergemann et al. (2025b) characterize the menu of token prices that maximizes a provider’s revenue across heterogeneous users. Our work also relates to a recent line that evaluates LLMs not only by their capabilities but also by the price users pay (Wang et al., 2024b; Zellinger and Thomson, 2025; Erol et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). This alternative view has very recently materialized in already-deployed platforms: some platforms publish provider rankings that explicitly factor in their prices, while others act as routers that lower the price by letting providers compete on their rates.1 In contrast to these solutions, our platform explicitly ensures that the user asymptotically pays the most competitive market price for their specific task at guaranteed quality levels.

Our work also builds on a large body of literature on mechanism and auction design (McAfee and McMillan, 1986; Ledyard, 1987; Che, 1993; Bar-Yossef et al., 2002; Roughgarden et al., 2017; Akbarpour and Li, 2020; Awaya et al., 2025; Cai and Liao, 2026). In this context, our sequential setting connects to a strand on dynamic auctions, where bidders sequentially learn private information, such as their type, that determines their utility, and the objective is to design mechanisms that ensure truthful bidding over multiple time steps (Hossain, 2008; Pavan et al., 2014; Weed et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2018; Bergemann and Välimäki, 2019; Bergemann et al., 2025a). To the best of our knowledge, however, we are the first to consider a setting where LLM providers act as bidders whose operational costs and serving qualities vary across tasks.

Lastly, at a technical level, our work relates to a strand of the multi-armed bandit literature in which the learner must choose among alternatives that are themselves strategic agents seeking to maximize their utility, requiring learning algorithms that explicitly account for these incentives (Auer et al., 2002; Even-Dar et al., 2006; Babaioff et al., 2009; Bubeck and Cesa-Bianchi, 2012; Jain et al., 2015; Braverman et al., 2019; Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020; Freeman et al., 2020; Padmanabhan et al., 2022). Therein, the closest works to ours are those that study procurement auctions through a bandit lens (Singla and Krause, 2013; Chen et al., 2026b; Patra et al., 2026). Specifically, both Chen et al. (2026b) and Patra et al. (2026) formulate procurement as a contextual bandit problem, with the latter studying the selection of LLM providers through a reverse auction where providers report their generation costs and the user learns query-dependent model quality. Unlike Patra et al. (2026), however, we do not assume that providers know their model’s cost on the user’s task, and our payment rule asymptotically converges to the most competitive price, equal to the second-lowest average cost among qualified providers. In a similar LLM routing setting, Cao et al. (2026) instead design an allocation and payment mechanism that disincentivizes providers from misreporting their capabilities or manipulating the token bills charged to the user.

2 A Procurement Platform for Reliable Inference

In this section, we introduce a procurement platform that acts as an intermediary between a user who seeks to solve a specific task (e.g., coding, mathematical reasoning, or question answering) and a set of NN LLM providers. By incentivizing providers to compete on price, the platform ensures the user secures the most competitive pricing at a guaranteed quality level on all but a vanishing fraction of queries.

The platform operates sequentially over time steps t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\dots,T, where the total number of queries TT is unknown to the providers but assumed to be at least the number of providers NN. At any given time step, each provider participates in the platform by maintaining a standing bid bi,t∈[0,cmax]b_{i,t}\in[0,c_{\max}], where cmax>0c_{\max}>0 is an upper bound on the cost of serving a single query. Given the current bid vector 𝐛t=(b1,t,…,bN,t)\mathbf{b}_{t}=(b_{1,t},\dots,b_{N,t}), the platform receives a query xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in\mathcal{X} that the user wishes to solve, where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the space of possible queries characterizing the user’s task, and selects the provider It∈[N]I_{t}\in[N] that serves it. Provider ItI_{t} generates a response yt∈𝒴y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y} to the query, where 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is the space of possible responses,33 3 In practice, the provider generates yty_{t} by sampling a sequence of tokens from its model, and so 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is the set of finite-length token sequences. and, by doing so, it incurs a generation cost cIt,t∈[0,cmax]c_{I_{t},t}\in[0,c_{\max}], which includes the cost of energy, compute, or hardware. The platform then grades the response using a score r⁡(xt,yt)∈[0,1]r(x_{t},y_{t})\in[0,1], ranging from unsatisfactory (0)(0) to fully satisfactory (1)(1), and sets the payment the user makes to provider ItI_{t}. Finally, provider ItI_{t} may update its standing bid to bIt,t+1b_{I_{t},t+1}, while the bid of every other provider remains unchanged: bi,t+1=bi,tb_{i,t+1}=b_{i,t} for all i≠Iti\neq I_{t}. In what follows, we denote the distribution of the query as PxP^{x}, the distribution of the cost incurred by provider ii as PicP^{c}_{i}, and the distribution of the score received by provider ii’s response as PirP^{r}_{i}, with a mean qi∈[0,1]q_{i}\in[0,1] that we refer to as the (average) quality of the provider.

We now describe the rules used by the platform to allocate queries and pay the providers. Our key idea is to combine an allocation rule based on confidence bounds—which progressively narrows the search to the qualified provider offering the lowest price to the user—with a second-price payment rule that incentivizes providers to bid as low as possible without risking an unprofitable win. Specifically, the platform begins with an initialization phase spanning the first NN time steps, during which it assigns one query to each provider in turn and pays them cmaxc_{\max}. This ensures every provider serves at least one query, rendering the estimates below well-defined from round N+1N+1 onward.

Thereafter, at each round t>Nt>N, the platform maintains a running estimate of each provider’s quality,

q^i,t=1mi,t∑τ=1t−1r(xτ,yτ) 1{Iτ=i},\hat{q}_{i,t}=\frac{1}{m_{i,t}}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1}r(x_{\tau},y_{\tau})\,\mathbbm{1}\{I_{\tau}=i\}, (1)

where mi,t=∑τ=1t−1𝟙{Iτ=i}m_{i,t}=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{\tau}=i\} counts how many times provider ii has been selected before round tt. The goal of these estimates is to identify the set of qualified providers 𝒬={i∈[N]:qi≥qmin}\mathcal{Q}=\{i\in[N]:q_{i}\geq q_{\min}\}, meeting a user-defined quality threshold qminq_{\min}, which we assume contains at least two providers44 4 This assumption is needed only for the analysis. If a single provider is estimated to be qualified, the minimum in Eq. 4 is over an empty set and the provider is paid cmaxc_{\max}.. Since the true qualities qiq_{i} are unknown, the platform instead forms an optimistic estimate of 𝒬\mathcal{Q},

To design the payment rule, we build on the classical second-price rule from the auction and mechanism design literature (Vickrey, 1961; Nisan et al., 2011). Specifically, for any provider ii, we define the critical payment Pi,tP_{i,t} as

Overall, the complete operation of our procurement platform is summarized in Algorithm 1.

3 Pricing Inference Through Competition

In this section, we study the incentives that providers face when participating in our procurement platform and characterize their optimal bidding strategy. As a first step, we analyze the conditions under which a provider is selected to serve a query as a function of their bid. Concretely, the following proposition shows that, when 𝒮t=∅\mathcal{S}_{t}=\emptyset, a provider’s assignment is determined by whether their standing bid falls below the critical payment Pi,tP_{i,t}.66 6 All proofs are deferred to Appendix A.

Proposition 1.

Fix a step t>Nt>N with 𝒮t=∅\mathcal{S}_{t}=\emptyset, a provider i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, and the other providers’ bids 𝐛−i,t\mathbf{b}_{-i,t}. Then, provider ii is assigned the query xtx_{t} if they bid bi,t<Pi,tb_{i,t}<P_{i,t}, and is not assigned the query if bi,t>Pi,tb_{i,t}>P_{i,t}.

The above proposition does not fully characterize how a provider should bid; however, it already offers valuable intuition. When 𝒮t≠∅\mathcal{S}_{t}\neq\emptyset, the query is assigned independently of the bids 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t}, meaning a provider’s bid only influences the allocation when 𝒮t=∅{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=\emptyset. In this case, a provider is assigned the query only if it bids below the threshold Pi,tP_{i,t}. Because this threshold depends on the other providers’ bids, it is unknown to provider ii in advance, which incentivizes it to bid as low as possible. Conversely, once a provider bids low enough to secure the query, due to the payment rule in Eq. 5, their final payout remains independent of their own bid. Together, these properties suggest that providers are incentivized to bid truthfully according to the generation costs they incur. In the remainder of this section, we formalize this intuition and characterize the resulting equilibrium.

We cast the interaction among the NN providers on the platform as a multi-stage game (Fudenberg and Tirole, 1991). In this game, each provider ii is characterized by its score and cost distributions θi=(Pir,Pic)\theta_{i}=(P^{r}_{i},P^{c}_{i}) on the user’s task, which need not be known even to the provider itself; we write 𝜽=(θ1,…,θN)\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}).77 7 In the game theory literature, this corresponds to an incomplete-information setting in which θi\theta_{i} is the (private) type of each provider (Harsanyi, 2004; Hossain, 2008; Feng et al., 2018). Moreover, its action in the game corresponds to choosing a bidding strategy σi\sigma_{i} that determines its standing bid bi,tb_{i,t} based on its observed history Hi,tH_{i,t}, which collects the costs ci,τc_{i,\tau} and scores r⁡(xτ,yτ)r(x_{\tau},y_{\tau}) of every query that provider ii has served before time step tt, i.e.,88 8 Our theoretical results also hold if each provider ii is allowed to use a time-varying bidding strategy σi,t\sigma_{i,t}. This is because, as we will show later, our notion of bidding strategy optimality applies to any arbitrary strategy at any time tt. However, to lighten the notation, we focus on time-invariant bidding strategies mapping histories to bids.

Having formalized the providers’ interaction as a game, we now turn to characterizing their equilibrium bidding strategies. Specifically, since a provider ii knows neither the score and cost distributions 𝜽−i\bm{\theta}_{-i} characterizing the other providers nor the total number of user queries TT, we focus on strategies that maximize its utility under this uncertainty using the framework of robust game theory (Aghassi and Bertsimas, 2006). Formally, the next theorem shows that the strategy σi∗\sigma_{i}^{*} that bids the provider’s cost estimate for the next query, i.e.,

σi∗​(Hi,t)=c^i,t,\sigma_{i}^{*}(H_{i,t})=\hat{c}_{i,t}, (8)

Theorem 2.

    for every σi\sigma_{i}, if 𝒮t=∅{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=\emptyset, i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} and (σi∗​(Hi,t)−Pi,t)​(σi​(Hi,t)−Pi,t)<0(\sigma^{*}_{i}(H_{i,t})-P_{i,t})(\sigma_{i}(H_{i,t})-P_{i,t})<0, the inequality in ii) is strict.

In the above theorem, claim i) states that σi∗\sigma^{*}_{i} never incurs an expected loss, and it holds because a provider bidding its cost estimate serves a query only when the payment covers that estimate. Claim ii) states that σi∗\sigma_{i}^{*} maximizes the worst-case utility, and it holds because a provider who does not know TT cannot rule out that the current query is the last one; consequently, the worst-case utility of any strategy is bounded above by its net payment from the current query. Moreover, under σi∗\sigma_{i}^{*}, the worst-case utility matches this upper bound exactly because, by claim i), no later query can reduce it. Since this worst-case scenario effectively isolates the current query, and because the payment does not depend on the provider’s own bid, the optimal bid is the lowest possible value that avoids an expected loss—which is precisely the provider’s cost estimate. Claim iii) states that any deviation changing whether the provider is assigned the query yields a strictly lower worst-case utility, and it holds because, if the current query happens to be the last one, such a deviation either causes the provider to forgo a profitable query or forces it to serve an unprofitable one.

Furthermore, as an immediate consequence of Theorem 2, the choice of bidding strategies 𝝈∗=(σ1∗,…,σN∗)\bm{\sigma}^{*}=(\sigma^{*}_{1},\dots,\sigma^{*}_{N}) is a robust equilibrium, i.e., for every σi\sigma_{i}

infT≥t,𝜽−iUi|Ht​(σi∗,𝝈−i∗,𝜽−i,T)≥infT≥t,𝜽−iUi|Ht​(σi,𝝈−i∗,𝜽−i,T).\inf_{T\geq t,\,\bm{\theta}_{-i}}U_{i\mid H_{t}}(\sigma^{*}_{i},\bm{\sigma}^{*}_{-i};\bm{\theta}_{-i},T)\;\geq\;\inf_{T\geq t,\,\bm{\theta}_{-i}}U_{i\mid H_{t}}(\sigma_{i},\bm{\sigma}^{*}_{-i};\bm{\theta}_{-i},T). (9)

In words, at every step t>Nt>N and after every history, no provider ii can improve its worst-case utility by deviating from σi∗\sigma^{*}_{i} when the other providers follow 𝝈−i∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}_{-i}.

4 Finding the Lowest Competitive Inference Price

In this section, we show that, when all providers choose their equilibrium strategy σi∗\sigma_{i}^{*}, the user is served by a provider meeting their quality threshold qminq_{\min} on all but a vanishing fraction of the queries, while the price they pay converges to the most competitive price the market can offer for their task. For concreteness, in the remainder of the section, we specify the function g⁡(t)g(t) to be of the form g⁡(t)=k​(t/N)αg(t)=k(t/N)^{\alpha}, where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and k>0k>0 are given parameters.

We begin by identifying the provider that serves most of the user’s queries. More precisely, we show that, on all but a vanishing fraction of queries, the platform selects the qualified provider i∗i^{*} with the lowest cost, i.e.,

i∗=argmini∈𝒬c¯i,i^{*}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{i\in\mathcal{Q}}\bar{c}_{i}, (10)

which we refer to as the optimal provider and assume to be unique. The number of queries not served by the optimal provider depends on the specific parameters α\alpha and kk chosen by the platform as well as on the difficulty of distinguishing each provider from i∗i^{*}, which we characterize using two quantities for each provider. First, for an unqualified provider i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q}, we let εi=qmin−qi>0\varepsilon_{i}=q_{\min}-q_{i}>0 measure how far its quality falls below the quality threshold. Second, for a qualified provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, we let Δi=c¯i−c¯i∗>0\Delta_{i}=\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}>0 measure how far its mean cost exceeds that of i∗i^{*}. Intuitively, the smaller εi\varepsilon_{i} or Δi\Delta_{i}, the harder the corresponding provider is to distinguish from i∗i^{*}, and the more queries the platform may allocate to them, as formalized in the next theorem.

Theorem 3.

When all providers choose their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the number of time steps in which the platform does not assign the query to the lowest-cost qualified provider, i.e., It≠i∗I_{t}\neq i^{*}, is at most N−1+Bid​(T)N-1+B_{\mathrm{id}}(T), where

Bid​(T)≔∑i∉𝒬M⁡(εi)+∑i∈𝒬∖{i∗}max⁡{M⁡(Δicmax),k⋅(TN)α},B_{\mathrm{id}}(T)\coloneqq\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M(\varepsilon_{i})+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\max\left\{M\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{i}}{c_{\max}}\right),\;k\cdot\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha}\right\}, (11)

where, for any x>0x>0,

M⁡(x)=⌈4x2​ln⁡(57​Nδ​x4)⌉.M(x)=\left\lceil\frac{4}{x^{2}}\,\ln\!\left(\frac{57N}{\delta x^{4}}\right)\right\rceil.

In the above theorem, the bound consists of the N−1N-1 initialization steps not served by i∗i^{*} alongside a sum of per-provider terms. For an unqualified provider, the term grows as 1/εi21/\varepsilon_{i}^{2} up to logarithmic factors. Conversely, for a qualified provider other than i∗i^{*}, the term is determined by the maximum of two terms: a term growing as 1/Δi21/\Delta_{i}^{2} that bounds the steps in which it outbids i∗i^{*} and a term k​(T/N)αk(T/N)^{\alpha} that bounds the exploration steps in which it is selected. Crucially, this bound depends sublinearly on the total number of queries TT. Hence, the platform allocates the query to the optimal provider on all but a vanishing fraction of the user’s queries.

We now turn to the price the user pays on the platform for a query, i.e., the payment πt\pi_{t} made to the provider serving it. More concretely, we focus on comparing this payment with the second-lowest mean cost among qualified providers, c¯(2)=mini∈𝒬∖{i∗}⁡c¯i\bar{c}_{(2)}=\min_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\bar{c}_{i}. This cost represents the most competitive (average) price the user could hope to pay for a query: it is the lowest price the optimal provider i∗i^{*} would need to offer to remain cheaper than every other qualified provider, since the next-cheapest cannot profitably offer a price below its own mean cost c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)}. The next theorem shows that the average payment converges to the second-lowest mean cost among qualified providers.

Theorem 4.

When all providers choose their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*} and the user submits a minimum number T0T_{0} of queries, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta the payments made by the user satisfy

1T​∑t=1T|πt−c¯(2)|≤\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr|\;\leq\; T0T​cmax+k​(NT)1−α​(cmax−c¯(2))\displaystyle\frac{T_{0}}{T}\,c_{\max}+k\left(\frac{N}{T}\right)^{\!1-\alpha}\bigl(c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)
+6​cmax2−α​12​k​(NT)α​ln⁡(2​π2​N​k23​δ​(TN)2​α),\displaystyle+\frac{6\,c_{\max}}{2-\alpha}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2k}\left(\frac{N}{T}\right)^{\!\alpha}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}Nk^{2}}{3\delta}\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!2\alpha}\right)}, (12)

where T0=N​max⁡{1,(M¯/k)1/α}T_{0}=N\max\bigl\{1,\,(\bar{M}/k)^{1/\alpha}\bigr\} and M¯=max⁡{1,maxi∉𝒬⁡M⁡(εi)}\bar{M}=\max\bigl\{1,\max_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M(\varepsilon_{i})\bigr\}. Hence, 1T​∑t=1Tπt→c¯(2)\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{t}\to\bar{c}_{(2)} as T→∞T\to\infty.

In the above theorem, the first term accounts for the first T0T_{0} time steps, which include the NN initialization steps and the non-exploration steps during which an unqualified provider may still belong to 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}; the second term accounts for the exploration steps after T0T_{0}, in which the selected provider is paid cmaxc_{\max}; and the third term accounts for the remaining steps. As TT grows, the average difference between the payment and the second-lowest mean cost c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)} of a qualified provider vanishes at a rate max{T−(1−α),T−α/2}\max\{T^{-(1-\alpha)},\,T^{-\alpha/2}\}, up to logarithmic factors. In Corollary 12 in Appendix A.9, we show that this rate is maximized when the platform sets α=2/3\alpha=2/3, giving a rate of T−1/3T^{-1/3}.

5 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate our platform on simulated providers serving real LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families. Specifically, we evaluate whether the platform learns the set of qualified providers and progressively routes queries to the optimal provider i∗i^{*}. We then compare the price paid on our platform against the average per-token price listed by inference providers on Hugging Face99 9 https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/index, consulted on December 30, 2025.. Appendix D and Appendices E–G contain further details on our experimental setup and additional experimental results, respectively.

Experimental setup. Each of the NN simulated providers serves one LLM, which we use to identify them. We consider two settings: (i) N=9N=9 providers, each serving a model from the Llama family (Llama-{3-8B, 3.1-8B, 3.2-1B, 3.2-3B}-Instruct) or the Qwen family (Qwen-{2-0.5B, 2-1.5B, 2-7B, 2.5-3B, 2.5-7B}-Instruct), and (ii) N=4N=4 providers serving the newest of the largest models and the smallest model of each family, i.e., Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2-0.5B.

In both settings, the user’s queries are drawn from one of two widely used benchmarks. In the setting with N=9N=9 providers, we draw queries from the GSM8K dataset (Cobbe et al., 2021), which consists of K=1,319K=1{,}319 grade-school mathematical reasoning problems. In the setting with N=4N=4 providers, we draw queries from the GPQA (Rein et al., 2024) dataset, which consists of K=546K=546 graduate-level science questions. Both benchmarks feature verifiable ground-truth answers, and the score r⁡(xt,yt)r(x_{t},y_{t}) represents whether the response is correct (1) or incorrect (0). Consequently, the quality qiq_{i} of a provider corresponds to the probability that the model generates a correct answer. We rely on a public dataset of recorded generations,1010 10 https://huggingface.co/datasets/Human-Centric-Machine-Learning/strategic-ttc-data which contains 128128 generations per model for every question across both benchmarks. In each experiment, we simulate T=70,000T=70{,}000 queries by taking 53.0753.07 and 128.21128.21 passes over all queries in GSM8K and GPQA, respectively, sampling without replacement. At each step, once a provider is selected, its response is sampled uniformly at random from its 128128 recorded generations for that query. We repeat each experiment across 3030 independent runs to report averaged results.

Since the public dataset we use lacks generation costs, we construct them using real-world market signals. In particular, the cost of each recorded generation is determined by its token count and the model’s average per-token price on the Hugging Face inference-provider list—on the order of $0.1\$0.1 per million tokens—discounted by a fixed 25%25\% margin (i.e., divided by 1.251.25), common to all providers and unknown to the platform (see Appendix D, Table 2). We define v¯i=1.25​c¯i\bar{v}_{i}=1.25\,\bar{c}_{i} as the mean query price of provider ii, representing the average amount a user pays per query under publicly listed prices. Further, we place the quality threshold qminq_{\min} at the midpoint between two adjacent provider qualities, so that three providers qualify on GSM8K and two on GPQA.

We purposely choose these two settings to vary the intensity of competition among qualified providers, which fundamentally determines the user’s final payment. Specifically, since the average payment converges to the second-lowest mean cost c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)} among qualified providers by Theorem 4, we call competition strong when c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)} is smaller than the listed query price of the optimal provider v¯i∗\bar{v}_{i^{*}}, and weak otherwise. On GSM8K, the qualified competitors of i∗i^{*} are considerably more expensive (c¯(2)>v¯i∗\bar{c}_{(2)}>\bar{v}_{i^{*}}, weak), whereas on GPQA, the sole competitor is only slightly more expensive (c¯(2)<v¯i∗\bar{c}_{(2)}<\bar{v}_{i^{*}}, strong). Table 1 summarizes both settings.

The platform runs Algorithm 1 with confidence level δ=0.05\delta=0.05 and exploration function g⁡(t)=k​(t/N)αg(t)=k(t/N)^{\alpha}, with k=2k=2 and α=3/4\alpha=3/4. We choose this value over the rate-optimal α=2/3\alpha=2/3 from Corollary 12 to induce greater early exploration at the expense of a slower asymptotic rate. Under this setup, the simulated providers follow their equilibrium strategy 𝝈∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}.

Results. Table 1 summarizes our main results. We find that the platform successfully identifies the optimal provider: over the final pass of the benchmark, it routes at least 96%96\% of all queries to i∗i^{*}, and i∗i^{*} becomes the most selected provider after roughly 10,00010{,}000 and 30,00030{,}000 queries on GSM8K and GPQA respectively. In both cases, this occurs well before the time step Tid=min⁡{T:T>N+2​Bid​(T)}T_{\mathrm{id}}=\min\{T\,:\,T>N+2B_{\mathrm{id}}(T)\}, i.e., the time step beyond which Theorem 3 guarantees, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, that i∗i^{*} is the unique most-selected provider (63,74063{,}740 and 153,697153{,}697 queries, respectively; see Appendices E.1 and G.1). This gap demonstrates that our sample complexity bounds are highly conservative in practice. The delayed convergence on GPQA stems from the presence of the unqualified Llama-3.2-1B model; because its quality falls a mere 0.0370.037 below qminq_{\min}, the platform requires approximately 11,00011{,}000 queries to statistically exclude it from 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}.

Figure 1 provides additional insight into the temporal evolution of the winning bids, payments and costs. In agreement with Theorem 4, we find that, for the initial queries, the payment on non-exploration steps lies below c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i^{*}}; this occurs because cheaper, unqualified providers that the platform has not yet excluded from 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} are still selected and influence the pricing mechanism. However, as the platform routes more queries, the payment converges towards c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)}. Importantly, we also find that the user’s payment for a guaranteed quality level is fundamentally determined by the intensity of competition among qualified providers on each benchmark. On the final pass, under strong competition on GPQA, the average payment per query on non-exploration steps lies 10%10\% above the generation cost c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i^{*}} and 12%12\% below the listed price v¯i∗\bar{v}_{i^{*}} that the user would pay in the current fixed-price market. Conversely, under weak competition on GSM8K, the average payment lies 71%71\% above c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i^{*}} and 37%37\% above v¯i∗\bar{v}_{i^{*}}, due to the higher cost of the nearest qualified competitor. Altogether, the results suggest that our platform allows users to pay a price that approaches the one supported by provider competition on their specific task, capturing substantial savings whenever the market-clearing price falls below public fixed listings.

6 Discussion and Limitations

In this section, we highlight several limitations of our work and discuss avenues for future research.

Methodology. We assume that a provider maximizes its worst-case utility by bidding its current cost estimate, since it knows neither the total number of user queries nor the score and cost distributions of its competitors. However, because providers may violate this assumption in practice, we extend our theoretical results in Appendix C to a setting where bids can deviate above or below the cost estimate by bounded amounts. In this context, analyzing our platform using other game-theoretic solution concepts remains an interesting direction for future work. Further, whenever the cost difference across providers is small, or the providers’ quality sits right on the threshold, our platform requires a relatively large number of queries to secure the best price for the user. In such cases, future work could lower query requirements by leveraging quality and cost estimates across tasks. Finally, in our platform, users carry the cost of exploration. However, because the most cost-competitive provider directly benefits from this exploration, one may argue that this burden should be shifted to, or at least shared with, the providers, who typically possess greater financial resources. Exploring alternative payment rules that redistribute such a burden represents an interesting direction for future work.

Evaluation. We evaluated our platform using simulated providers who compete to serve queries from benchmarking datasets with verifiable ground truth. An important next step would be to evaluate our platform in settings where providers compete to serve open-ended queries and quality is measured automatically without relying on predefined correct outputs. Further, in our experiments, we estimated the generation costs by discounting publicly listed token prices by a fixed 25%25\% profit margin. Future research should leverage specialized profiling tools to measure these true costs precisely. Ultimately, deploying and evaluating the proposed platform in a real-world production environment remains crucial.

Practical considerations. We assume that our platform can accurately estimate the quality of the responses generated by the providers. In many domains where LLMs are routinely used, such as coding or mathematical reasoning, automated evaluation procedures make this feasible with minimal overhead. Moving forward, the viability of our platform in settings with less well-established quality metrics and benchmarks will depend on continued progress in the LLM evaluation literature. Lastly, we note that, while second-price auctions possess many desirable properties, they also make a provider’s payment dependent on the bids of its competitors. This dependence leaves the mechanism potentially vulnerable to manipulation or collusion (Hendricks and Porter, 1989; Mailath and Zemsky, 1991; Che et al., 2018).

7 Conclusions

In this work, we introduced a procurement platform that connects large language model providers with end-users, where token prices are driven by provider competition via reverse second-price auctions. More concretely, this mechanism incentivizes providers to truthfully bid their best estimate of the average cost to serve a user’s query. We demonstrated that, with high probability, the platform routes all but a vanishing fraction of the user’s queries to the most cost-competitive provider meeting a desired quality threshold. Moreover, this provider’s average pricing margin converges to the difference between the second-lowest average cost among such providers and its own average cost. Empirically, we demonstrated that the pricing margin on our platform varies significantly—from 10%10\% to 71%71\%—depending on the task and quality threshold, revealing a substantial inefficiency in the current fixed-price market. Ultimately, we hope that our work inspires users, providers, and routing platforms to explore alternative, more efficient economic paradigms for the market of LLM-as-a-service.

Appendix A Proofs

A.1 Concentration inequalities for the qualities and costs

In this section, we characterize the relationship between the estimated confidence sets 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, introduced in Eq. 2, and the set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of qualified providers. To this end, we first define a high-probability event under which, for every provider and every selection count, the empirical quality and cost averages are simultaneously close to their corresponding population averages. For each provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and m≥1m\geq 1, let q^i,m\hat{q}_{i,m} and c^i,m\hat{c}_{i,m} denote the empirical means of the scores and generation costs observed over the first mm queries served by provider ii, respectively. Recall that

β⁡(m)=12​m​ln⁡(2​π2​N​m23​δ).\beta(m)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2m}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}Nm^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}.
Lemma 1.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the event that, simultaneously for every provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and every m≥1m\geq 1,

|q^i,m−qi|≤β⁡(m),|c^i,m−c¯i|≤cmax​β​(m).\left|\hat{q}_{i,m}-q_{i}\right|\leq\beta(m),\qquad\left|\hat{c}_{i,m}-\bar{c}_{i}\right|\leq c_{\max}\beta(m). (13)

Then, Pr⁡(ℰ)≥1−δ\Pr(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta.

Proof.

Fix a provider i∈[N]i\in[N], and let τi​(1)<τi​(2)<⋯\tau_{i}(1)<\tau_{i}(2)<\cdots denote the steps in which provider ii is selected. Since the platform selects a provider before the score and generation cost of that step are realized, the successive observations

r⁡(xτi​(1),yτi​(1)),r⁡(xτi​(2),yτi​(2)),…r(x_{\tau_{i}(1)},y_{\tau_{i}(1)}),r(x_{\tau_{i}(2)},y_{\tau_{i}(2)}),\ldots

are i.i.d. draws from 𝒫ir\mathcal{P}_{i}^{r} with mean qiq_{i}, and the successive realized costs

ci,τi​(1),ci,τi​(2),…c_{i,\tau_{i}(1)},c_{i,\tau_{i}(2)},\ldots

are i.i.d. draws from 𝒫ic\mathcal{P}_{i}^{c} with mean c¯i\bar{c}_{i}. Thus, for every fixed selection count m≥1m\geq 1, Hoeffding’s inequality and the fact that scores lie in [0,1][0,1] give

Pr⁡(|q^i,m−qi|>β⁡(m))≤2​exp⁡(−2​m​β​(m)2).\Pr\!\left(\left|\hat{q}_{i,m}-q_{i}\right|>\beta(m)\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-2m\beta(m)^{2}\right).

Similarly, since generation costs lie in [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}],

Pr⁡(|c^i,m−c¯i|>cmax​β​(m))≤2​exp⁡(−2​m​β​(m)2).\Pr\!\left(\left|\hat{c}_{i,m}-\bar{c}_{i}\right|>c_{\max}\beta(m)\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-2m\beta(m)^{2}\right).

By the definition of β⁡(m)\beta(m),

2​exp⁡(−2​m​β​(m)2)=3​δπ2​N​m2.2\exp\!\left(-2m\beta(m)^{2}\right)=\frac{3\delta}{\pi^{2}Nm^{2}}.

A union bound over the two estimates, all providers, and all selection counts therefore gives

Pr⁡(ℰc)\displaystyle\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{c}) ≤∑i=1N∑m=1∞2​3​δπ2​N​m2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2\frac{3\delta}{\pi^{2}Nm^{2}}
=6​δπ2​∑m=1∞1m2=δ,\displaystyle=\frac{6\delta}{\pi^{2}}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m^{2}}=\delta,

where ∑m=1∞m−2=π2/6\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}m^{-2}=\pi^{2}/6. Hence,

Pr⁡(ℰ)≥1−δ.\Pr(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta.

∎

We next prove a technical result showing that a lower bound on the confidence radius β⁡(m)\beta(m) implies an upper bound on the selection count mm. We will use this result in the proof of Lemma 7 and Lemma 8.

Lemma 2.

For any a>0a>0 and m≥1m\geq 1, if

a≤2​β​(m),a\leq 2\beta(m), (14)

then

m≤4a2​ln⁡(57​Nδ​a4).m\leq\frac{4}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57N}{\delta a^{4}}\right). (15)
Proof.

By (14) and the definition of β⁡(m)\beta(m),

12​m​ln⁡(2​π2​N​m23​δ)≥a24.\frac{1}{2m}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}Nm^{2}}{3\delta}\right)\geq\frac{a^{2}}{4}.

m≤2a2​ln⁡(2​π2​N​m23​δ)=2a2​ln⁡(2​π2​N3​δ)+4a2​ln⁡m.m\leq\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}Nm^{2}}{3\delta}\right)=\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}N}{3\delta}\right)+\frac{4}{a^{2}}\ln m.

so that m≤A+B​ln⁡mm\leq A+B\ln m. For every r>0r>0, the inequality ln⁡x≤x−1\ln x\leq x-1 gives

Hence,

(1−Br)​m≤A+B⁡(ln⁡r−1).\left(1-\frac{B}{r}\right)m\leq A+B(\ln r-1).

Therefore,

=4a2​[ln⁡(2​π2​N3​δ)+2​ln⁡(8a2)−2]\displaystyle=\frac{4}{a^{2}}\left[\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}N}{3\delta}\right)+2\ln\!\left(\frac{8}{a^{2}}\right)-2\right]
=4a2​ln⁡(128​π2​N3​e2​δ​a4)\displaystyle=\frac{4}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{128\pi^{2}N}{3e^{2}\delta a^{4}}\right)
≤4a2​ln⁡(57​Nδ​a4),\displaystyle\leq\frac{4}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57N}{\delta a^{4}}\right),

where the final inequality follows from 128​π2/(3​e2)<57128\pi^{2}/(3e^{2})<57. ∎

A.2 Properties of exploration steps

We next establish several basic properties of the allocation rule that will be used when proving the theoretical results stated in Section 3 and Section 4.

Lemma 3.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, every qualified provider remains in the estimated-qualified set at every post-initialization step:

𝒬⊆𝒬^t,t>N.\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t},\qquad t>N. (16)

In particular, 𝒬^t≠∅\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\neq\emptyset for every t>Nt>N.

Proof.

Fix i∈𝒬i\in\mathcal{Q} and t>Nt>N. Since ii is qualified,

qi≥qmin.q_{i}\geq q_{\min}.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, Lemma 1 gives, for any provider ii and time step t>Nt>N,

q^i,t≥qi−β⁡(mi,t).\hat{q}_{i,t}\geq q_{i}-\beta(m_{i,t}).

Therefore,

q^i,t+β⁡(mi,t)≥qi≥qmin,\hat{q}_{i,t}+\beta(m_{i,t})\geq q_{i}\geq q_{\min},

and hence i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} by the definition of the estimated-qualified set. Since this holds for every i∈𝒬i\in\mathcal{Q}, we obtain 𝒬⊆𝒬^t\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}. Finally, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} contains at least two providers by assumption, so 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} is nonempty under the event ℰ\mathcal{E}. ∎

Lemma 4.

Suppose that g:ℕ→ℝg\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} is non-decreasing, and fix a total number of user queries T>NT>N. If provider ii is selected in an exploration step t≤Tt\leq T, then

mi,t<g⁡(t)≤g⁡(T).m_{i,t}<g(t)\leq g(T). (17)

Consequently, provider ii can be selected in an exploration step at most

⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1 (18)

times, and the total number of post-initialization exploration steps up to TT queries is at most

N⁡(⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1).N\left(\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1\right). (19)
Proof.

If provider ii is selected in an exploration step tt, then i∈𝒮ti\in\mathcal{S}_{t}. By definition of 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t},

mi,t<g⁡(t).m_{i,t}<g(t).

Since gg is non-decreasing and t≤Tt\leq T,

mi,t<g⁡(t)≤g⁡(T),m_{i,t}<g(t)\leq g(T),

which proves (17).

Now suppose that tt is an exploration step in which provider ii is selected. Since mi,tm_{i,t} is a positive integer after initialization, (17) implies

mi,t≤⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1.m_{i,t}\leq\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1.

Thus, provider ii can therefore be selected in an exploration step at most ⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1\lceil g(T)\rceil-1 when the total number of user queries is TT. Summing this bound over all NN providers gives (19). ∎

A.3 Properties of non-exploration steps

We next establish properties of the allocation rule on non-exploration steps, that is, when 𝒮t=∅\mathcal{S}_{t}=\emptyset and the selection of provider ItI_{t} depends on the bids 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t}. We begin by proving Proposition 1.

Proof of Proposition 1.

Proof of Proposition 1.

Fix a time step t>Nt>N with 𝒮t=∅\mathcal{S}_{t}=\emptyset, a provider i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, and the other providers’ bids 𝐛−i,t\mathbf{b}_{-i,t}. Since tt is not an exploration step, the allocation rule (Eq. 3) selects a provider minimizing the adjusted bid

bj,t−cmax​β​(mj,t)b_{j,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t}) (20)

over j∈𝒬^tj\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}.

Provider ii is therefore selected whenever

bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)<minj∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj,t−cmax​β​(mj,t)).b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})<\min_{j\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\left(b_{j,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t})\right).

Rearranging gives

bi,t<cmax​β​(mi,t)+minj∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj,t−cmax​β​(mj,t))=Pi,t,b_{i,t}<c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})+\min_{j\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\left(b_{j,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t})\right)=P_{i,t},

where the equality follows from the definition of Pi,tP_{i,t}. Thus bi,t<Pi,tb_{i,t}<P_{i,t} implies that provider ii is selected.

Similarly, if

bi,t>Pi,t,b_{i,t}>P_{i,t},

then

bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)>minj∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj,t−cmax​β​(mj,t)).b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})>\min_{j\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\left(b_{j,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t})\right).

so provider ii does not minimize the adjusted bid and is therefore not selected. This proves the claim. ∎

Lemma 5.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, for every provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and every step t>Nt>N,

c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯i.\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\bar{c}_{i}. (21)
Proof.

Fix a provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and a step t>Nt>N. Under the equilibrium strategy σ∗\sigma^{*},

bi,t=c^i,t.b_{i,t}=\hat{c}_{i,t}.

Thus, on ℰ\mathcal{E},

c¯i−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c^i,t≤c¯i+cmax​β​(mi,t).\bar{c}_{i}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\hat{c}_{i,t}\leq\bar{c}_{i}+c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}). (22)

Substituting bi,t=c^i,tb_{i,t}=\hat{c}_{i,t} and subtracting cmax​β​(mi,t)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}) yields

c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯i.\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\bar{c}_{i}.

which proves the claim. ∎

Lemma 6.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, if a provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} is selected at a non-exploration step t>Nt>N, then

Δi≤2​cmax​β​(mi,t),\Delta_{i}\leq 2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}), (23)

where Δi=c¯i−c¯i∗>0\Delta_{i}=\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}>0.

Proof.

Fix a non-exploration step t>Nt>N in which i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} is selected. Under the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, Lemma 3 implies that i∗∈𝒬^ti^{*}\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}. Since tt is a non-exploration step, the allocation rule therefore implies

bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi∗,t−cmax​β​(mi∗,t).b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i^{*},t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i^{*},t}).

Applying Lemma 5 to both providers gives

c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi∗,t−cmax​β​(mi∗,t)≤c¯i∗.\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i^{*},t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i^{*},t})\leq\bar{c}_{i^{*}}.

Hence,

c¯i−c¯i∗≤2​cmax​β​(mi,t).\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}\leq 2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}).

Since Δi=c¯i−c¯i∗\Delta_{i}=\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}, this proves (23). ∎

Lemma 7.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, if a provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} is selected at a non-exploration step t>Nt>N, then

mi,t≤Li≔⌈4​cmax2Δi2​ln⁡(57​N​cmax4δ​Δi4)⌉.m_{i,t}\leq L_{i}\coloneqq\left\lceil\frac{4c_{\max}^{2}}{\Delta_{i}^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57Nc_{\max}^{4}}{\delta\Delta_{i}^{4}}\right)\right\rceil. (24)

Consequently, once mi,t>Lim_{i,t}>L_{i}, provider ii cannot be selected at a non-exploration step

Proof.

By Lemma 6, if provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} is selected at a non-exploration step t>Nt>N, then

Δi≤2​cmax​β​(mi,t).\Delta_{i}\leq 2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}).

Dividing by cmaxc_{\max} gives

Δicmax≤2​β​(mi,t).\frac{\Delta_{i}}{c_{\max}}\leq 2\beta(m_{i,t}).

Applying Lemma 2 with

a=Δicmaxa=\frac{\Delta_{i}}{c_{\max}}

therefore yields

mi,t≤4​cmax2Δi2​ln⁡(57​N​cmax4δ​Δi4)≤Li.m_{i,t}\leq\frac{4c_{\max}^{2}}{\Delta_{i}^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57Nc_{\max}^{4}}{\delta\Delta_{i}^{4}}\right)\leq L_{i}.

Thus, if mi,t>Lim_{i,t}>L_{i}, provider ii cannot be selected by the allocation rule at a non-exploration step. ∎

A.4 Elimination of unqualified providers

We next bound the number of times an unqualified provider can be selected on the platform, including both non-exploration and exploration steps.

Lemma 8.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, every unqualified provider i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q}, with quality gap

εi≔qmin−qi>0,\varepsilon_{i}\coloneqq q_{\min}-q_{i}>0,

is selected at most

Mi≔⌈4εi2​ln⁡(57​Nδ​εi4)⌉M_{i}\coloneqq\left\lceil\frac{4}{\varepsilon_{i}^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57N}{\delta\varepsilon_{i}^{4}}\right)\right\rceil (25)

times in post-initialization steps.

Proof.

Fix an unqualified provider i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} and a post-initialization step t>Nt>N in which It=iI_{t}=i. Whether tt is a non-exploration or exploration step, provider ii can be selected only if i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}. Hence,

q^i,t+β⁡(mi,t)≥qmin.\hat{q}_{i,t}+\beta(m_{i,t})\geq q_{\min}.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, Lemma 1 gives

q^i,t≤qi+β⁡(mi,t).\hat{q}_{i,t}\leq q_{i}+\beta(m_{i,t}).

Combining the two inequalities yields

qmin≤qi+2​β​(mi,t),q_{\min}\leq q_{i}+2\beta(m_{i,t}),

and therefore

εi≤2​β​(mi,t).\varepsilon_{i}\leq 2\beta(m_{i,t}). (26)

Applying Lemma 2 with a=εia=\varepsilon_{i} gives

mi,t≤4εi2​ln⁡(57​Nδ​εi4)≤Mi.m_{i,t}\leq\frac{4}{\varepsilon_{i}^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57N}{\delta\varepsilon_{i}^{4}}\right)\leq M_{i}.

Since this holds whenever provider ii is selected in a post-initialization step, provider ii is selected at most MiM_{i} times after initialization. Consequently, once mi,t>Mim_{i,t}>M_{i}, provider ii cannot be selected at any step t>Nt>N. ∎

A.5 Selection and identification bounds

We now bound the total number of times a qualified suboptimal provider can be selected.

Lemma 9.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, for every provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, the number of post-initialization steps t≤Tt\leq T in which It=iI_{t}=i is at most

max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1},\max\left\{L_{i},\,\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1\right\}, (27)

where LiL_{i} is defined in Lemma 7.

Proof.

Fix T>NT>N and a provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, and consider any post-initialization step t≤Tt\leq T in which It=iI_{t}=i. If tt is a non-exploration step, Lemma 7 gives

mi,t≤Li.m_{i,t}\leq L_{i}.

If instead tt is an exploration step, Lemma 4 gives

mi,t<g⁡(t)≤g⁡(T).m_{i,t}<g(t)\leq g(T).

Since mi,tm_{i,t} is an integer,

mi,t≤⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1.m_{i,t}\leq\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1.

Thus, in either case,

mi,t≤max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}.m_{i,t}\leq\max\left\{L_{i},\,\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1\right\}.

Since provider ii is selected once during initialization and mi,tm_{i,t} increases by one at each of its selections, its ℓ\ell-th post-initialization selection occurs at a step tt with mi,t=ℓm_{i,t}=\ell. Hence, provider ii is selected at most max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}\max\{L_{i},\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\} times in post-initialization steps t≤Tt\leq T. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.

We work under the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, which by Lemma 1 occurs with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. In the first NN initialization steps, each provider is selected exactly once. Hence, at most N−1N-1 initialization steps are not assigned to i∗i^{*}.

We next consider the post-initialization steps. Every provider i≠i∗i\neq i^{*} is either unqualified or qualified and suboptimal. By Lemma 8, each provider i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} is selected at most

Mi=⌈4εi2​ln⁡(57​Nδ​εi4)⌉=M⁡(εi)M_{i}=\left\lceil\frac{4}{\varepsilon_{i}^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{57N}{\delta\varepsilon_{i}^{4}}\right)\right\rceil=M(\varepsilon_{i})

times after initialization.

For each provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, Lemma 9 gives at most

max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}\max\left\{L_{i},\,\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1\right\}

post-initialization selections, where Li=M⁡(Δi/cmax)L_{i}=M(\Delta_{i}/c_{\max}) by Lemma 7 and, for

g⁡(t)=k​(tN)α,g(t)=k\left(\frac{t}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha},

we have ⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1=⌈k​(T/N)α⌉−1\lceil g(T)\rceil-1=\lceil k(T/N)^{\alpha}\rceil-1.

Since every step with It≠i∗I_{t}\neq i^{*} selects exactly one provider other than i∗i^{*}, summing these bounds and adding the N−1N-1 initialization steps gives

∑t=1T𝟙{It≠i∗}\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\neq i^{*}\} ≤N−1+∑i∉𝒬Mi+∑i∈𝒬∖{i∗}max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}\displaystyle\leq N-1+\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M_{i}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\max\left\{L_{i},\,\left\lceil g(T)\right\rceil-1\right\}
=N−1+∑i∉𝒬M⁡(εi)+∑i∈𝒬∖{i∗}max⁡{M⁡(Δicmax),⌈k​(TN)α⌉−1}\displaystyle=N-1+\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M(\varepsilon_{i})+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\max\left\{M\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{i}}{c_{\max}}\right),\;\left\lceil k\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha}\right\rceil-1\right\}
≤N−1+Bid​(T),\displaystyle\leq N-1+B_{\mathrm{id}}(T),

which proves the claimed bound. ∎

Corollary 5.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

1T∑t=1T𝟙{It≠i∗}⟶0as T→∞.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\neq i^{*}\}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{as }T\to\infty. (28)

In particular, the platform assigns a fraction tending to one of the user’s queries to the lowest-cost qualified provider i∗i^{*}.

Proof.

On the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, Theorem 3 gives

∑t=1T𝟙{It≠i∗}≤N−1+∑i∉𝒬Mi+∑i∈𝒬∖{i∗}max{Li,k(TN)α}.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\neq i^{*}\}\leq N-1+\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M_{i}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\max\left\{L_{i},\,k\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha}\right\}.

Dividing by TT yields

1T∑t=1T𝟙{It≠i∗}≤N−1+∑i∉𝒬MiT+1T∑i∈𝒬∖{i∗}max{Li,k(TN)α}.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\neq i^{*}\}\leq\frac{N-1+\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M_{i}}{T}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\max\left\{L_{i},\,k\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha}\right\}.

The quantities MiM_{i} and LiL_{i} are independent of TT. Moreover, since α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

k​(T/N)αT=kNα​Tα−1→T→∞0.\frac{k(T/N)^{\alpha}}{T}=\frac{k}{N^{\alpha}}T^{\alpha-1}\xrightarrow{T\to\infty}0.

Hence every term on the right-hand side converges to zero, which proves (28). Since Pr⁡(ℰ)≥1−δ\Pr(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta by Lemma 1, the result holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. ∎

Corollary 6.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, if at some step t>Nt>N,

mi,t>Mifor every ​i∉𝒬,andmi,t>Lifor every ​i∈𝒬∖{i∗},m_{i,t}>M_{i}\quad\text{for every }i\notin\mathcal{Q},\qquad\text{and}\qquad m_{i,t}>L_{i}\quad\text{for every }i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, (29)

then every non-exploration step τ≥t\tau\geq t is assigned to the optimal provider i∗i^{*}.

Proof.

Fix an ordinary step τ≥t\tau\geq t. Since selection counts are non-decreasing,

mi,τ>Mifor every ​i∉𝒬,mi,τ>Lifor every ​i∈𝒬∖{i∗}.m_{i,\tau}>M_{i}\quad\text{for every }i\notin\mathcal{Q},\qquad m_{i,\tau}>L_{i}\quad\text{for every }i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}.

By Lemma 8, no unqualified provider can be selected at step τ\tau. By Lemma 7, no qualified provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} can be selected at non-exploration step τ\tau. Finally, Lemma 3 guarantees that i∗∈𝒬^τi^{*}\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}. Hence, in a non-exploration step, the allocation rule must select i∗i^{*}. ∎

A.6 Generic cumulative counting and confidence-radius bounds

In this section, we establish a bound on sums of confidence radii along the sequence of selected providers. This counting argument is independent of whether a step is exploratory or non-exploratory and will be used in the proof of Theorem 7.

Lemma 10 (Radius sum).

Fix T≥NT\geq N and let (at)t=N+1T(a_{t})_{t=N+1}^{T} be nonnegative numbers satisfying

at≤κβ(mIt,t),t=N+1,…,T,a_{t}\leq\kappa\,\beta(m_{I_{t},t}),\qquad t=N+1,\ldots,T,

for some κ≥0\kappa\geq 0. Then,

∑t=N+1Tat≤κ​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}a_{t}\leq\kappa\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}. (30)
Proof.

For each provider i∈[N]i\in[N], let

Di=mi,T+1−1D_{i}=m_{i,T+1}-1

denote the number of times provider ii is selected after initialization up to and including time step TT. Since exactly one provider is selected at every post-initialization step,

∑i=1NDi=T−N.\sum_{i=1}^{N}D_{i}=T-N.

Therefore,

∑t=N+1Tat\displaystyle\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}a_{t} ≤κ​∑i=1N∑ℓ=1Diβ⁡(ℓ)\displaystyle\leq\kappa\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\ell=1}^{D_{i}}\beta(\ell)
=κ​∑i=1N∑ℓ=1Di12​ℓ​ln⁡(2​π2​N​ℓ23​δ).\displaystyle=\kappa\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\ell=1}^{D_{i}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\ell}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}N\ell^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}.

Since ℓ≤Di≤T\ell\leq D_{i}\leq T,

β⁡(ℓ)≤12​ℓ​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\beta(\ell)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\ell}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}.

Hence,

∑t=N+1Tat\displaystyle\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}a_{t} ≤κ​12​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ)​∑i=1N∑ℓ=1Di1ℓ\displaystyle\leq\kappa\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\ell=1}^{D_{i}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ell}}
≤κ​2​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ)​∑i=1NDi,\displaystyle\leq\kappa\sqrt{2\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{D_{i}},

where we used ∑ℓ=1Dℓ−1/2≤2D\sum_{\ell=1}^{D}\ell^{-1/2}\leq 2\sqrt{D}. Finally, using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

∑i=1NDi≤N​∑i=1NDi=N⁡(T−N).\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{D_{i}}\leq\sqrt{N\sum_{i=1}^{N}D_{i}}=\sqrt{N(T-N)}.

Combining the preceding inequalities gives

∑t=N+1Tat≤κ​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ),\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}a_{t}\leq\kappa\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)},

as claimed. ∎

A.7 User performance guarantees

We now derive the quality guarantees that the user obtains on the platform.

Theorem 7.

On the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, the sum

RTqual=∑t=1T(qmin−qIt)+,R_{T}^{\mathrm{qual}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(q_{\min}-q_{I_{t}}\bigr)^{+},

which measures the cumulative quality under qminq_{\min} obtained by the user, satisfies,

RTqual≤min⁡{N+2​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ),∑i∉𝒬(Mi+1)​εi}.R_{T}^{\mathrm{qual}}\leq\min\left\{N+2\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)},\;\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}\bigl(M_{i}+1\bigr)\varepsilon_{i}\right\}. (31)

Moreover, the number of queries assigned to unqualified providers satisfies,

∑t=1T𝟙{It∉𝒬}≤∑i∉𝒬(Mi+1).\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\notin\mathcal{Q}\}\leq\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}(M_{i}+1). (32)

Consequently,

RTqualT=O(1T)⟶0,1T∑t=1T𝟙{It∉𝒬}=O(1T)⟶0\frac{R_{T}^{\mathrm{qual}}}{T}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\notin\mathcal{Q}\}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)\longrightarrow 0 (33)
Proof.

In the first NN initialization steps, every provider is selected once. Since (qmin−qi)+≤1(q_{\min}-q_{i})^{+}\leq 1, the contribution of the first NN steps to the sum RTqualR_{T}^{\mathrm{qual}} is at most NN.

Consider now a post-initialization step t>Nt>N. If It∈𝒬I_{t}\in\mathcal{Q}, then qIt≥qminq_{I_{t}}\geq q_{\min} and the step does not contribute to the sum RTqualR_{T}^{\mathrm{qual}}. If It∉𝒬I_{t}\notin\mathcal{Q}, then the selected provider must belong to 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}. In the proof of Lemma 8 (Eq. 26), we showed that this implies that:

εIt=(qmin−qIt)+≤2​β​(mIt,t).\varepsilon_{I_{t}}=\bigl(q_{\min}-q_{I_{t}}\bigr)^{+}\leq 2\beta(m_{I_{t},t}).

Applying Lemma 10 with κ=2\kappa=2 therefore gives

∑t=N+1T(qmin−qIt)+≤2​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}\bigl(q_{\min}-q_{I_{t}}\bigr)^{+}\leq 2\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}.

Adding the initialization contribution proves the first bound in (31).

Alternatively, Lemma 8, the elimination bound for unqualified providers, shows that every i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} is selected at most MiM_{i} times after initialization. Including its initialization selection, provider ii therefore contributes at most

(Mi+1)​εi(M_{i}+1)\varepsilon_{i}

to the cumulative quality regret. Summing over all i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} proves the second bound in (31).

The same selection bound immediately gives

∑t=1T𝟙{It∉𝒬}≤∑i∉𝒬(Mi+1).\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\notin\mathcal{Q}\}\leq\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}(M_{i}+1).

proving (32).

Finally, the right-hand sides of the second bound in (31) and of (32) are independent of TT. Dividing both inequalities by TT therefore gives (33). ∎

We next bound the cumulative excess mean generation cost of the selected providers relative to the optimal provider i∗i^{*}, i.e., how much more the user’s queries cost to serve than they would if every query were served by i∗i^{*}. We refer to this quantity as the generation-cost regret.

Theorem 8.

Suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. On the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, the sum

RTgen=∑t=1T(c¯It−c¯i∗)+R_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(\bar{c}_{I_{t}}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}\bigr)^{+}

satisfies

RTgen≤min{\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}\leq\min\Biggl\{ (N−1)​⌈g⁡(T)⌉​cmax+2​cmax​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ),\displaystyle(N-1)\lceil g(T)\rceil c_{\max}+2c_{\max}\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)},
∑i∉𝒬(Mi+1)(c¯i−c¯i∗)++∑i∈𝒬∖{i∗}(max{Li,⌈g(T)⌉−1}+1)Δi}.\displaystyle\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}(M_{i}+1)\bigl(\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}\bigr)^{+}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}}\bigl(\max\{L_{i},\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\}+1\bigr)\Delta_{i}\Biggr\}. (34)
Proof.

Since every mean cost lies in [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}], each term of RTgenR_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}} is at most cmaxc_{\max}, and it vanishes whenever It=i∗I_{t}=i^{*}.

For the first bound, we partition the time steps up to TT into initialization steps, exploration steps, and non-exploration steps. During initialization, at most N−1N-1 steps are not assigned to i∗i^{*}, which contribute at most (N−1)​cmax(N-1)c_{\max}. By Lemma 4, every provider is selected in at most ⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1\lceil g(T)\rceil-1 exploration steps, so the exploration steps assigned to a provider other than i∗i^{*} contribute at most (N−1)​(⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1)​cmax(N-1)(\lceil g(T)\rceil-1)c_{\max}. Finally, consider a non-exploration step t>Nt>N with It=i≠i∗I_{t}=i\neq i^{*}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, Lemma 3 gives i∗∈𝒬^ti^{*}\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, so the allocation rule (Eq. 3) implies

bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi∗,t−cmax​β​(mi∗,t),b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i^{*},t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i^{*},t}),

and Lemma 5, applied to both providers, yields c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\bar{c}_{i^{*}}. Hence, letting at=(c¯It−c¯i∗)+a_{t}=(\bar{c}_{I_{t}}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}})^{+} on non-exploration steps and at=0a_{t}=0 on exploration steps, we have at≤2​cmax​β​(mIt,t)a_{t}\leq 2c_{\max}\beta(m_{I_{t},t}) for every t=N+1,…,Tt=N+1,\ldots,T, and Lemma 10 with κ=2​cmax\kappa=2c_{\max} gives

∑t=N+1Tat≤2​cmax​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}a_{t}\leq 2c_{\max}\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}.

Summing the three contributions proves the first bound.

For the second bound, Lemma 8 shows that every i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} is selected at most MiM_{i} times after initialization, and Lemma 9 shows that every i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} is selected at most max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}\max\{L_{i},\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\} times after initialization. Including its initialization selection, each provider i≠i∗i\neq i^{*} therefore contributes at most its number of selections times (c¯i−c¯i∗)+(\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}})^{+} to RTgenR_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}, where (c¯i−c¯i∗)+=Δi(\bar{c}_{i}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}})^{+}=\Delta_{i} for i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}. Summing over i≠i∗i\neq i^{*} proves the second bound. ∎

A.8 Payments on exploration and non-exploration steps

We next bound the payments made by the user. On an exploration step, the selected provider is paid cmaxc_{\max}, whereas on an non-exploration step the payment is determined by the adjusted bid of the cheapest competing eligible provider.

Lemma 11.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, suppose that all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*}. For every non-exploration step t>Nt>N with It=iI_{t}=i,

πt≤min⁡{cmax,c¯(2)+cmax​β​(mi,t)}.\pi_{t}\leq\min\left\{c_{\max},\bar{c}_{(2)}+c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\right\}. (35)

Consequently,

(πt−c¯(2))+≤cmax​β​(mi,t).\bigl(\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)^{+}\leq c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}). (36)
Proof.

Fix a non-exploration step t>Nt>N with It=iI_{t}=i. Then, the payment rule (Eq. 5) gives

πt=min⁡{cmax​β​(mi,t)+minj∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj,t−cmax​β​(mj,t)),cmax}.\pi_{t}=\min\left\{c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})+\min_{j\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\left(b_{j,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t})\right),c_{\max}\right\}.

If i=i∗i=i^{*}, let jj be a second-cheapest qualified provider, so that c¯j=c¯(2)\bar{c}_{j}=\bar{c}_{(2)}. If i≠i∗i\neq i^{*}, let j=i∗j=i^{*}, in which case c¯j=c¯i∗≤c¯(2)\bar{c}_{j}=\bar{c}_{i^{*}}\leq\bar{c}_{(2)}. In either case, j∈𝒬j\in\mathcal{Q} and j≠ij\neq i and j∈𝒬^tj\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} on the event ℰ\mathcal{E}. Moreover, using Lemma 5,

bj,t−cmax​β​(mj,t)≤c¯j≤c¯(2).b_{j,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t})\leq\bar{c}_{j}\leq\bar{c}_{(2)}.

Therefore,

minj′∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj′,t−cmax​β​(mj′,t))≤c¯(2),\min_{j^{\prime}\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\left(b_{j^{\prime},t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{j^{\prime},t})\right)\leq\bar{c}_{(2)},

and hence

πt≤min⁡{cmax,c¯(2)+cmax​β​(mi,t)}.\pi_{t}\leq\min\left\{c_{\max},\bar{c}_{(2)}+c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\right\}.

The second claim follows immediately. ∎

Theorem 9.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, when all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*},

∑t=1T(πt−c¯(2))+≤\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)^{+}\leq\; [N+N⁡(⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1)]​(cmax−c¯(2))\displaystyle\left[N+N\bigl(\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\bigr)\right]\bigl(c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)
+cmax​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\displaystyle\quad+c_{\max}\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}. (37)
Proof.

Partition the time steps up to TT into initialization steps, exploration steps, and non-exploration steps.

During initialization, each of the NN providers is paid cmaxc_{\max}, so the total excess payment contributed by these steps is

N⁡(cmax−c¯(2)).N\bigl(c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr).

On every exploration step, the selected provider is also paid cmaxc_{\max}. By Lemma 4, there are at most N⁡(⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1)N(\lceil g(T)\rceil-1) such steps. Their total contribution is therefore at most

N⁡(⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1)​(cmax−c¯(2)).N\bigl(\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\bigr)\bigl(c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr).

Finally, on every non-exploration step t>Nt>N, Lemma 11 gives

(πt−c¯(2))+≤cmax​β​(mIt,t).\bigl(\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)^{+}\leq c_{\max}\beta(m_{I_{t},t}).

Hence, for the non-exploration steps, applying Lemma 10,

∑t=N+1t​non-explorationT(πt−c¯(2))+\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t=N+1\\ t\text{non-exploration}\end{subarray}}^{T}\bigl(\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)^{+} ≤cmax​∑t=N+1Tβ⁡(mIt,t)\displaystyle\leq c_{\max}\sum_{t=N+1}^{T}\beta(m_{I_{t},t})
≤cmax​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\displaystyle\leq c_{\max}\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}.

Summing the three contributions proves (37). ∎

Corollary 10.

Suppose

g⁡(t)=k​(tN)α,k>0,α∈(0,1).g(t)=k\left(\frac{t}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha},\qquad k>0,\quad\alpha\in(0,1).

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, when all providers use their equilibrium strategy 𝛔∗\bm{\sigma}^{*},

1T​∑t=1T(πt−c¯(2))+≤\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)^{+}\leq\; (NT+k​(NT)1−α)​(cmax−c¯(2))\displaystyle\left(\frac{N}{T}+k\left(\frac{N}{T}\right)^{1-\alpha}\right)\bigl(c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)
+cmax​2​NT​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ).\displaystyle\quad+c_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{2N}{T}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}. (38)
Proof.

Since

g⁡(T)=k​(TN)α,g(T)=k\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha},

the forced exploration term in Theorem 9 satisfies

N⁡(⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1)≤N​g​(T)=k​N​(TN)αN\bigl(\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\bigr)\leq Ng(T)=kN\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!\alpha} (39)

Substituting this into (37) and dividing by TT gives

N​g​(T)T=k​(NT)1−α\frac{Ng(T)}{T}=k\left(\frac{N}{T}\right)^{\!1-\alpha}

which proves the result. ∎

A.9 Payment convergence

We finally show that, on non-exploration steps, the payment converges to c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)}. Throughout, we write

M¯=max⁡{1,maxi∉𝒬⁡Mi},T0=N​max⁡{1,(M¯/k)1/α}\bar{M}=\max\bigl\{1,\max_{i\notin\mathcal{Q}}M_{i}\bigr\},\qquad T_{0}=N\max\bigl\{1,(\bar{M}/k)^{1/\alpha}\bigr\}

so that every time step t>T0t>T_{0} comes after initialization and satisfies g⁡(t)>M¯g(t)>\bar{M}

Lemma 12.

For every real x≥1x\geq 1, let

β⁡(x)=12​x​ln⁡(2​π2​N​x23​δ).\beta(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2x}\ln\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}Nx^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}. (40)

Then β\beta is decreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty). Consequently, β⁡(m)≤β⁡(x)\beta(m)\leq\beta(x) for every m≥x≥1m\geq x\geq 1.

Proof.

Let C=2​π2​N/(3​δ)C=2\pi^{2}N/(3\delta) and h⁡(x)=β​(x)2=ln⁡(C​x2)/(2​x)≥0h(x)=\beta(x)^{2}=\ln(Cx^{2})/(2x)\geq 0. Since 𝒬⊆[N]\mathcal{Q}\subseteq[N] contains at least two providers, N≥2N\geq 2. Since moreover δ<1\delta<1, for every x≥1x\geq 1,

C​x2≥C>4​π23>e2.Cx^{2}\geq C>\frac{4\pi^{2}}{3}>e^{2}.

Differentiating gives

h′​(x)=2−ln⁡(C​x2)2​x2<0,h^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2-\ln(Cx^{2})}{2x^{2}}<0,

so hh is decreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty), and so is β=h\beta=\sqrt{h}. ∎

Lemma 13.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, for every unqualified provider i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} and every step t>Nt>N, if i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, then

mi,t≤Mi.m_{i,t}\leq M_{i}.
Proof.

Fix i∉𝒬i\notin\mathcal{Q} and a step t>Nt>N with i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}. By the definition of estimated-qualified set and Lemma 1,

qmin≤q^i,t+β⁡(mi,t)≤qi+2​β​(mi,t),q_{\min}\leq\hat{q}_{i,t}+\beta(m_{i,t})\leq q_{i}+2\beta(m_{i,t}),

A.10 Robust optimality of the truthful strategy

Throughout, we fix a provider i∈[N]i\in[N], the strategies 𝝈−i\bm{\sigma}_{-i} of the other providers, and a history HtH_{t} of the platform before step t>Nt>N, containing the observed history Hi,tH_{i,t} of provider ii. For every step s≥ts\geq t, we write

Gi,s=(πs−c^i,s) 1{Is=i}G_{i,s}=\bigl(\pi_{s}-\hat{c}_{i,s}\bigr)\,\mathbbm{1}\{I_{s}=i\}

for the net payment of provider ii at step ss, so that Ui|Ht​(σi,𝝈−i,𝜽−i,T)=𝔼⁡[∑s=tTGi,s|Ht]U_{i\mid H_{t}}(\sigma_{i},\bm{\sigma}_{-i};\bm{\theta}_{-i},T)=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{s=t}^{T}G_{i,s}\,|\,H_{t}] by Eq. 7.

The proof rests on a single observation: once the history before a step is fixed, the net payment of provider ii at that step depends on its own bid only through whether it is assigned the query, and bidding the cost estimate is the best choice.

If 𝒮s=∅{\mathcal{S}}_{s}=\emptyset and i∉𝒬^i\notin\hat{\mathcal{Q}}, provider ii is not selected whatever it bids, so Gi,s​(b)=0G_{i,s}(b)=0 for every bb and all three claims hold.
