infT≥t,𝜽−iUi|Ht​(σi∗,T)=𝔼⁡[Gi,t​(c^i,t)|Ht].\inf_{T\geq t,\,\bm{\theta}_{-i}}U_{i\mid H_{t}}(\sigma_{i}^{*};T)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[G_{i,t}(\hat{c}_{i,t})\,|\,H_{t}\bigr]. (50)

Now fix any strategy σi\sigma_{i} and let b=σi​(Hi,t)b=\sigma_{i}(H_{i,t}) be its bid at step tt. Taking T=tT=t in the infimum and then applying Lemma 17b) for every realization of the platform’s draw at step tt,

infT≥t,𝜽−iUi|Ht​(σi,T)≤Ui|Ht​(σi,t)=𝔼⁡[Gi,t​(b)|Ht]≤𝔼⁡[Gi,t​(c^i,t)|Ht].\inf_{T\geq t,\,\bm{\theta}_{-i}}U_{i\mid H_{t}}(\sigma_{i};T)\leq U_{i\mid H_{t}}(\sigma_{i};t)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[G_{i,t}(b)\,|\,H_{t}\bigr]\leq\mathbb{E}\bigl[G_{i,t}(\hat{c}_{i,t})\,|\,H_{t}\bigr]. (51)

Combining Eqs. 50 and 51 proves claim ii).

Claim iii). Under the assumptions of claim iii), step tt is not an exploration step, so Gi,t​(b)G_{i,t}(b) and Gi,t​(c^i,t)G_{i,t}(\hat{c}_{i,t}) are determined by HtH_{t}, and Lemma 17c) gives Gi,t​(b)<Gi,t​(c^i,t)G_{i,t}(b)<G_{i,t}(\hat{c}_{i,t}). The last inequality in Eq. 51 is therefore strict, and so is the inequality in claim ii). ∎

Appendix B Bayesian cost estimation

The analysis in Appendix A considers providers that bid the empirical mean c^i,t\hat{c}_{i,t} of their observed generation costs. In this section, we show that the robust optimality of bidding one’s current cost estimate (Theorem 2) holds verbatim for any estimator, and that the user-facing guarantees of Section 4 extend to Bayesian estimators whose prior is eventually dominated by the data, with the cost-estimation radius widened by a factor 1+γ1+\gamma and unchanged asymptotic rates. No proof of Appendix A is repeated; instead, we identify the properties of the bids that those proofs use and verify them for Bayesian estimates.

Estimation model.

Each provider i∈[N]i\in[N] forms its cost estimate through a map eie_{i} from histories to [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}], and we write ei,t=ei​(Hi,t)e_{i,t}=e_{i}(H_{i,t}) for its estimate before step tt. Since Hi,tH_{i,t} consists of the first mi,tm_{i,t} observations of provider ii, we also write ei,me_{i,m} for the estimate after mm selections, so that ei,t=ei,mi,te_{i,t}=e_{i,m_{i,t}}, in the same way that q^i,t=q^i,mi,t\hat{q}_{i,t}=\hat{q}_{i,m_{i,t}} and c^i,t=c^i,mi,t\hat{c}_{i,t}=\hat{c}_{i,m_{i,t}}. For a Bayesian provider, ei,me_{i,m} is the posterior mean of the cost of serving its next query given a prior and its mm observed costs; it lies in [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}] because the cost does. We require that the prior does not pull the estimate away from the empirical mean by more than a fixed multiple of the confidence radius.

Assumption 1.

There exists a constant γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 such that, for every provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and every m≥1m\geq 1,

|ei,m−c^i,m|≤γ​cmax​β​(m).\bigl|e_{i,m}-\hat{c}_{i,m}\bigr|\leq\gamma\,c_{\max}\,\beta(m). (52)

The constant γ\gamma is a property of the estimation rule, and γ=0\gamma=0 recovers the empirical mean.

Lemma 18.

Under Assumption 1, on the event ℰ\mathcal{E} of Lemma 1, for every provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and every m≥1m\geq 1,

|ei,m−c¯i|≤(1+γ)​cmax​β​(m).\bigl|e_{i,m}-\bar{c}_{i}\bigr|\leq(1+\gamma)\,c_{\max}\,\beta(m). (53)
Proof.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, |c^i,m−c¯i|≤cmax​β​(m)|\hat{c}_{i,m}-\bar{c}_{i}|\leq c_{\max}\beta(m) by Eq. 13. By the triangle inequality and Eq. 52,

|ei,m−c¯i|≤|ei,m−c^i,m|+|c^i,m−c¯i|≤γ​cmax​β​(m)+cmax​β​(m).∎\bigl|e_{i,m}-\bar{c}_{i}\bigr|\leq\bigl|e_{i,m}-\hat{c}_{i,m}\bigr|+\bigl|\hat{c}_{i,m}-\bar{c}_{i}\bigr|\leq\gamma c_{\max}\beta(m)+c_{\max}\beta(m).\qed

Bayesian variant of the mechanism.

The platform uses a known upper bound γ\gamma satisfying Assumption 1—any larger valid bound may be used, since Eq. 52 is monotone in γ\gamma—and replaces the cost-estimation radius cmax​β​(mi,t)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}) by (1+γ)​cmax​β​(mi,t)(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}) in the adjusted bids of the allocation rule (Eq. 3) and in the critical payment (Eq. 4), i.e.,

It\displaystyle I_{t} =argmini∈𝒬^t(bi,t−(1+γ)​cmax​β​(mi,t)),\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{i\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}}\bigl(b_{i,t}-(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\bigr), if ​𝒮t=∅,\displaystyle\text{if }{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=\emptyset, (54)
Pi,t\displaystyle P_{i,t} =(1+γ)​cmax​β​(mi,t)+minj∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj,t−(1+γ)​cmax​β​(mj,t)).\displaystyle=(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})+\min_{j\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\bigl(b_{j,t}-(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t})\bigr).

The quality estimates q^i,t\hat{q}_{i,t}, the estimated-qualified set 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, the exploration set 𝒮t{\mathcal{S}}_{t}, the schedule gg, the initialization and exploration payments cmaxc_{\max}, and the payment cap in Eq. 5 are unchanged, and γ=0\gamma=0 recovers the mechanism of Section 2. Providers bid their current estimate, bi,t=ei,tb_{i,t}=e_{i,t}, and the utility in Eq. 7 is evaluated with ei,se_{i,s} in place of c^i,s\hat{c}_{i,s}.

The widening of the radius is necessary: if the platform kept cmax​βc_{\max}\beta, the adjusted bid of i∗i^{*} would only satisfy bi∗,t−cmax​β​(mi∗,t)≤c¯i∗+γ​cmax​β​(mi∗,t)b_{i^{*},t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i^{*},t})\leq\bar{c}_{i^{*}}+\gamma c_{\max}\beta(m_{i^{*},t}), and the optimism property bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯ib_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\bar{c}_{i} on which Lemma 6 rests would fail.

Proposition 13.

Consider the Bayesian variant of the mechanism in Eq. 54 with all providers bidding bi,t=ei,tb_{i,t}=e_{i,t}, and let Li(γ)=M⁡(Δi/((1+γ)​cmax))L_{i}^{(\gamma)}=M\bigl(\Delta_{i}/((1+\gamma)c_{\max})\bigr), where M⁡(⋅)M(\cdot) is defined in Theorem 3.

  1. i)

    Without Assumption 1: Lemmas 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 10, 12, 13,  14, and  15, Theorem 7, and the quantities MiM_{i}, M¯\bar{M}, and T0T_{0} hold exactly as stated, under arbitrary bids; and Proposition 1, Lemma 17, Theorem 2, and the robust-equilibrium property that follows it hold with ei,te_{i,t} in place of c^i,t\hat{c}_{i,t}, for any estimator eie_{i} with values in [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}].

  2. ii)

    Under Assumption 1: Lemmas 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, and 16, Theorems 3, 8, 9, 11, and 4, and Corollaries 5, 6, 10, and 12 hold after replacing each cost-estimation radius cmax​β​(⋅)c_{\max}\beta(\cdot) by (1+γ)​cmax​β​(⋅)(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(\cdot) in their statements, with the corresponding replacement Li→Li(γ)L_{i}\to L_{i}^{(\gamma)}.

Proof.

Claim i). The results in the first group concern the quality estimates, the estimated-qualified set, the exploration rule, or the confidence radius alone; their proofs do not involve the bids or the cost estimates, all of which the Bayesian variant leaves unchanged, so they hold as stated under arbitrary bids. For the second group, the proofs of Proposition 1 and Lemma 17 use only that the allocation rule selects a minimizer of bj,t−ρj,tb_{j,t}-\rho_{j,t} over 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} and pays min⁡{Pi,t,cmax}\min\{P_{i,t},c_{\max}\} with Pi,t=ρi,t+minj∈𝒬^t∖{i}⁡(bj,t−ρj,t)P_{i,t}=\rho_{i,t}+\min_{j\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}(b_{j,t}-\rho_{j,t}), for arbitrary radii ρj,t≥0\rho_{j,t}\geq 0 determined by the history, together with the fact that the bid compared to Pi,tP_{i,t} and the estimate entering the net payment Gi,sG_{i,s} coincide and lie in [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}]. Both hold for ρj,t=(1+γ)​cmax​β​(mj,t)\rho_{j,t}=(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{j,t}) and ei,t∈[0,cmax]e_{i,t}\in[0,c_{\max}]. The proof of Theorem 2 uses only Lemma 17 and that the truthful strategy bids the estimate entering Eq. 7 at every step. None of these proofs uses the event ℰ\mathcal{E} or the form of the estimator.

Claim ii). The only property of the bids used in the listed proofs is the adjusted-bid bound of Lemma 5, which in the Bayesian variant reads, on ℰ\mathcal{E} and by Lemma 18,

c¯i−2​(1+γ)​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi,t−(1+γ)​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯i,\bar{c}_{i}-2(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i,t}-(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\bar{c}_{i}, (55)

with the same one-line proof. Downstream of this bound, the radius enters only through the choice a=Δi/cmaxa=\Delta_{i}/c_{\max} in the application of Lemma 2 (proof of Lemma 7), which becomes a=Δi/((1+γ)​cmax)a=\Delta_{i}/((1+\gamma)c_{\max}) and yields Li(γ)L_{i}^{(\gamma)}, and the choices κ=cmax\kappa=c_{\max} and κ=2​cmax\kappa=2c_{\max} in the applications of Lemma 10 (proofs of Theorems 9 and 8), which become κ=(1+γ)​cmax\kappa=(1+\gamma)c_{\max} and κ=2​(1+γ)​cmax\kappa=2(1+\gamma)c_{\max}; both lemmas hold for arbitrary a>0a>0 and κ≥0\kappa\geq 0. Every other occurrence of cmaxc_{\max} in these proofs—the bid range, the initialization and exploration payments, the payment cap, the bound |πt−c¯(2)|≤cmax|\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}|\leq c_{\max}, and the factor cmax−c¯(2)c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}—refers to the range of costs and payments, which is unchanged. Hence each listed proof goes through verbatim under the stated replacement. ∎

Resulting guarantees.

Two consequences of Proposition 13ii) are worth recording. First, Theorem 3 holds with M⁡(Δi/cmax)M(\Delta_{i}/c_{\max}) replaced by Li(γ)=M⁡(Δi/((1+γ)​cmax))L_{i}^{(\gamma)}=M\bigl(\Delta_{i}/((1+\gamma)c_{\max})\bigr): the ordinary-step selection threshold of a qualified suboptimal provider grows with γ\gamma, while the terms for unqualified providers, the exploration term, and the quality guarantee of Theorem 7 are unchanged. Second, Theorem 4 holds with the coefficient 6​cmax2−α\frac{6\,c_{\max}}{2-\alpha} of its last term replaced by 6​(1+γ)​cmax2−α\frac{6(1+\gamma)\,c_{\max}}{2-\alpha}, and its first two terms unchanged; likewise, Lemma 16 gives c¯(2)−3​(1+γ)​cmax​β​(g⁡(t))≤πt≤c¯(2)+(1+γ)​cmax​β​(g⁡(t))\bar{c}_{(2)}-3(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(g(t))\leq\pi_{t}\leq\bar{c}_{(2)}+(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(g(t)) on every non-exploration step t>T0t>T_{0}. Hence, for fixed γ\gamma, the average absolute deviation of the payments from c¯(2)\bar{c}_{(2)} is O(T−(1−α))+O((1+γ)T−α/2ln⁡T)O\bigl(T^{-(1-\alpha)}\bigr)+O\bigl((1+\gamma)\,T^{-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\ln T}\bigr), the exponent is still maximized at α=2/3\alpha=2/3 (Corollary 12), and 1T​∑t=1Tπt→c¯(2)\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{t}\to\bar{c}_{(2)} as T→∞T\to\infty. The average excess-payment bound of Corollary 10 receives the same radius substitution in its last term only.

Provider incentives.

By Proposition 13i), bidding one’s current cost estimate, σi∗​(Hi,t)=ei,t\sigma_{i}^{*}(H_{i,t})=e_{i,t}, is worst-case optimal in the sense of Theorem 2 for any estimator with values in [0,cmax][0,c_{\max}], in the Bayesian variant of the mechanism as well as in the original one. The robust-optimality result is thus estimator-agnostic: once a provider’s utility is evaluated relative to its current estimate, the threshold structure of the allocation rule makes bidding that estimate optimal. Assumption 1 plays no role in this result; it is needed only to relate the providers’ estimates to their true mean costs, and thereby obtain the user-facing guarantees above.

Appendix C Robustness to deviations from cost-estimate bidding

Theorem 2 shows that, for a provider, bidding its current cost estimate is worst-case optimal, but a provider may nevertheless deviate from it. In this section, we quantify how the user-facing guarantees of Section 4 change when bids may fall below or above the cost estimate by bounded amounts.

Assumption 2.

There exist constants d−,d+≥0d_{-},d_{+}\geq 0 such that every provider i∈[N]i\in[N] follows a strategy σi\sigma_{i} with

−d−≤σi​(Hi,t)−c^i,t≤d+for every history ​Hi,t,t>N.-d_{-}\;\leq\;\sigma_{i}(H_{i,t})-\hat{c}_{i,t}\;\leq\;d_{+}\qquad\text{for every history }H_{i,t},\ t>N. (56)

The constant d−d_{-} bounds underbidding and d+d_{+} overbidding relative to the empirical mean cost; the equilibrium strategy 𝝈∗\bm{\sigma}^{*} of Eq. 8 is the case d−=d+=0d_{-}=d_{+}=0.

The good-event, quality-estimation, and forced-exploration results of Appendix A do not use the providers’ bids. In particular, Lemmas 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 10, 12, 13,  14, and  15, Theorem 7, and the quantities MiM_{i}, M¯\bar{M}, and T0T_{0} hold under Assumption 2 exactly as stated; unqualified providers are therefore eliminated, and the quality guarantee holds, unchanged. The remaining results depend on the bids only through Lemma 5, whose counterpart under deviations is the following:

Lemma 19.

Under Assumption 2, on the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, for every provider i∈[N]i\in[N] and step t>Nt>N,

c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)−d−≤bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯i+d+.\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})-d_{-}\;\leq\;b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\;\leq\;\bar{c}_{i}+d_{+}. (57)
Proof.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, |c^i,t−c¯i|≤cmax​β​(mi,t)|\hat{c}_{i,t}-\bar{c}_{i}|\leq c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t}) by Eq. 13; combine with c^i,t−d−≤bi,t≤c^i,t+d+\hat{c}_{i,t}-d_{-}\leq b_{i,t}\leq\hat{c}_{i,t}+d_{+}. ∎

The adjusted bid is no longer optimistic, since its upper bound exceeds c¯i\bar{c}_{i} by d+d_{+}, and its lower bound is lowered by d−d_{-}. Tracing these two shifts through the proofs of Appendix A gives the results below.

Selection and identification.

Underbidding by a competitor and overbidding by i∗i^{*} both help the competitor win a non-exploration round, so the two deviations enter the selection analysis.

Proposition 14.

Under Assumption 2, on the event ℰ\mathcal{E}:

  1. i)

    On every non-exploration step t>Nt>N, the selected provider satisfies

    c¯It−c¯i∗≤ 2​cmax​β​(mIt,t)+d−+d+.\bar{c}_{I_{t}}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}}\;\leq\;2c_{\max}\beta(m_{I_{t},t})+d_{-}+d_{+}. (58)
  2. ii)

    Every qualified provider i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\} with Δi>d−+d+\Delta_{i}>d_{-}+d_{+} is selected after initialization at most max⁡{Li(d),⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}\max\{L_{i}^{(d)},\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\} times, where

    Li(d)≔M⁡(Δi−d−−d+cmax)L_{i}^{(d)}\;\coloneqq\;M\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{i}-d_{-}-d_{+}}{c_{\max}}\right) (59)

    and M⁡(⋅)M(\cdot) is defined in Theorem 3.

  3. iii)

    If Δi>d−+d+\Delta_{i}>d_{-}+d_{+} for every i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, then Theorem 3 and Corollaries 5 and 6 hold with M⁡(Δi/cmax)M(\Delta_{i}/c_{\max}) replaced by Li(d)L_{i}^{(d)}.

Proof.

Claim i). As in the proof of Lemma 6: on ℰ\mathcal{E}, i∗∈𝒬^ti^{*}\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} by Lemma 3, so the selected provider It=iI_{t}=i satisfies bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)≤bi∗,t−cmax​β​(mi∗,t)b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq b_{i^{*},t}-c_{\max}\beta(m_{i^{*},t}). Bounding the left side from below and the right side from above with Eq. 57 gives c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)−d−≤c¯i∗+d+\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})-d_{-}\leq\bar{c}_{i^{*}}+d_{+}. This holds for every i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, qualified or not, since Eq. 57 holds for every provider.

Claim ii). At every non-exploration selection of i∈𝒬∖{i∗}i\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{i^{*}\}, claim i) gives (Δi−d−−d+)/cmax≤2​β​(mi,t)(\Delta_{i}-d_{-}-d_{+})/c_{\max}\leq 2\beta(m_{i,t}), and Lemma 2 with a=(Δi−d−−d+)/cmax>0a=(\Delta_{i}-d_{-}-d_{+})/c_{\max}>0 gives mi,t≤Li(d)m_{i,t}\leq L_{i}^{(d)}. The rest is the proof of Lemma 9 with LiL_{i} replaced by Li(d)L_{i}^{(d)}.

Claim iii). The proofs of Theorem 3 and its corollaries use the bids only through Lemma 9, which claim ii) replaces. ∎

The condition Δi>d−+d+\Delta_{i}>d_{-}+d_{+} cannot be dropped: if Δi≤d−+d+\Delta_{i}\leq d_{-}+d_{+}, the bids bi,t=c^i,t−d−b_{i,t}=\hat{c}_{i,t}-d_{-} and bi∗,t=c^i∗,t+d+b_{i^{*},t}=\hat{c}_{i^{*},t}+d_{+} satisfy Assumption 2 and, once the two providers have comparable selection counts, give ii an adjusted bid at most that of i∗i^{*} up to the confidence radii, so ii may win every ordinary round. When some qualified competitor is within d−+d+d_{-}+d_{+} of i∗i^{*}, the platform therefore need not identify i∗i^{*}; claim i) shows what it guarantees instead: on every ordinary round it selects a provider whose mean cost exceeds c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i^{*}} by at most d−+d+d_{-}+d_{+} plus a vanishing term, and that provider is qualified on all but the rounds bounded by Lemma 8.

Theorem 15.

Under Assumption 2, on the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, the generation-cost regret of Theorem 8 satisfies

RTgen≤(N−1)​⌈g⁡(T)⌉​cmax+2​cmax​2​N​(T−N)​ln⁡(2​π2​N​T23​δ)+(d−+d+)​(T−N).R_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}\;\leq\;(N-1)\lceil g(T)\rceil c_{\max}+2c_{\max}\sqrt{2N(T-N)\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}NT^{2}}{3\delta}\right)}+(d_{-}+d_{+})(T-N). (60)

In the proof of the first bound of Theorem 8, the inequality c¯i−2​cmax​β​(mi,t)≤c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i}-2c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})\leq\bar{c}_{i^{*}} on non-exploration steps is replaced by Eq. 58. Payments.

Overbidding and underbidding affect the two sides of the payment bounds separately: the payment is set by the adjusted bid of the cheapest competing provider, which overbidding raises by at most d+d_{+} and underbidding lowers by at most d−d_{-}.

Lemma 20.

Under Assumption 2, on the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, on every non-exploration step t>Nt>N with It=iI_{t}=i,

πt≤min⁡{cmax,c¯(2)+cmax​β​(mi,t)+d+},\pi_{t}\;\leq\;\min\bigl\{c_{\max},\;\bar{c}_{(2)}+c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})+d_{+}\bigr\}, (61)

and, if moreover t>T0t>T_{0},

cmax​β​(mi,t)+Ai∗,t\displaystyle c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})+A_{i^{*},t} ≥cmax​β​(mi,t)+Ai,t=bi,t≥c^i,t−d−\displaystyle\geq c_{\max}\beta(m_{i,t})+A_{i,t}=b_{i,t}\geq\hat{c}_{i,t}-d_{-}
≥c¯i−cmax​β​(g⁡(t))−d−≥c¯(2)−cmax​β​(g⁡(t))−d−\displaystyle\geq\bar{c}_{i}-c_{\max}\beta(g(t))-d_{-}\geq\bar{c}_{(2)}-c_{\max}\beta(g(t))-d_{-}

At d−=d+=0d_{-}=d_{+}=0, Eqs. 61 and 62 are Lemmas 11 and 16.

Theorem 16.

Under Assumption 2, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for every T≥T0T\geq T_{0},

1T​∑t=1T|πt−c¯(2)|\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr| ≤T0T​cmax+k​(NT)1−α​(cmax−c¯(2))+max⁡{d−,d+}\displaystyle\leq\frac{T_{0}}{T}\,c_{\max}+k\left(\frac{N}{T}\right)^{\!1-\alpha}\bigl(c_{\max}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\bigr)+\max\{d_{-},d_{+}\}
+6​cmax2−α​12​k​(NT)α​ln⁡(2​π2​N​k23​δ​(TN)2​α)\displaystyle\quad+\frac{6\,c_{\max}}{2-\alpha}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2k}\left(\frac{N}{T}\right)^{\!\alpha}\ln\!\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}Nk^{2}}{3\delta}\left(\frac{T}{N}\right)^{\!2\alpha}\right)} (63)

and consequently

c¯(2)−d−≤lim infT→∞1T​∑t=1Tπt≤lim supT→∞1T​∑t=1Tπt≤c¯(2)+d+.\bar{c}_{(2)}-d_{-}\;\leq\;\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{t}\;\leq\;\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{t}\;\leq\;\bar{c}_{(2)}+d_{+}. (64)

Moreover, the average excess payment of Corollary 10 is bounded by its right-hand side plus d+d_{+}.

Proof.

In the proof of Theorem 11, the only change is on the non-exploration steps t>T0t>T_{0}, where Lemma 20 gives |πt−c¯(2)|≤3​cmax​β​(g⁡(t))+max⁡{d−,d+}|\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}|\leq 3c_{\max}\beta(g(t))+\max\{d_{-},d_{+}\} in place of 3​cmax​β​(g⁡(t))3c_{\max}\beta(g(t)); summing the additional term over at most TT steps and dividing by TT gives Eq. 63. For Eq. 64, the same decomposition applied to πt−c¯(2)\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)} without absolute values gives, for the non-exploration steps t>T0t>T_{0}, −3​cmax​β​(g⁡(t))−d−≤πt−c¯(2)≤cmax​β​(g⁡(t))+d+-3c_{\max}\beta(g(t))-d_{-}\leq\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)}\leq c_{\max}\beta(g(t))+d_{+}, while the first T0T_{0} steps and the exploration steps contribute O⁡(T0/T+T−(1−α))O(T_{0}/T+T^{-(1-\alpha)}) to the average; the vanishing terms are those of Eq. 63. The excess-payment claim follows from Eq. 61 in the proof of Theorem 9, whose ⋅\sqrt{\cdot} term is unchanged and which acquires the additional term d+​(T−N)d_{+}(T-N). ∎

Summary.

Under bounded deviations, the platform still serves qualified providers on all but a bounded number of rounds; it identifies i∗i^{*} whenever every qualified competitor is more than d−+d+d_{-}+d_{+} costlier, and otherwise selects a qualified provider within d−+d+d_{-}+d_{+} of c¯i∗\bar{c}_{i^{*}} in mean cost; and the average payment converges to within [c¯(2)−d−,c¯(2)+d+][\bar{c}_{(2)}-d_{-},\ \bar{c}_{(2)}+d_{+}] at the rate of Theorem 4. Underbidding thus affects the lower side of the payment guarantee by at most d−d_{-}, whereas overbidding affects the upper side by at most d+d_{+}; neither affects the quality guarantee, and both slow identification through the reduced gaps Δi−d−−d+\Delta_{i}-d_{-}-d_{+}. Setting d−=d+=0d_{-}=d_{+}=0 recovers Theorems 3, 8, and 4 verbatim. Finally, for the Bayesian variant of Appendix B, with Assumption 2 stated relative to ei,te_{i,t} in place of c^i,t\hat{c}_{i,t}, the same statements hold with cmax​β​(⋅)c_{\max}\beta(\cdot) replaced by (1+γ)​cmax​β​(⋅)(1+\gamma)c_{\max}\beta(\cdot) throughout and Li(d)L_{i}^{(d)} replaced by M⁡((Δi−d−−d+)/((1+γ)​cmax))M\bigl((\Delta_{i}-d_{-}-d_{+})/((1+\gamma)c_{\max})\bigr), since the proofs above use the empirical mean only through Eq. 13, which Lemma 18 replaces.

Appendix D Experimental details

In this section, we describe the experimental setup we use to evaluate our platform (Algorithm 1). Here, our goal is twofold: first, to instantiate the model of Section 2 using recorded generations from real LLMs, so that provider qualities and generation costs are grounded in observed data; and second, to compare the platform against practical routing policies that a platform could deploy today. In what follows, we describe the data, the construction of providers, the experimental settings, the routing policies we compare against, and the metrics we report.

Recorded generation data.

We evaluate the platform using a publicly available dataset of recorded LLM generations.1111 11 https://huggingface.co/datasets/Human-Centric-Machine-Learning/strategic-ttc-data The data cover GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and GPQA (Rein et al., 2024), spanning a wide range of difficulty. For every model–question pair, the data contain 128 recorded generations, each annotated with a binary correctness label, an output-token count, and, when needed for Best-of-nin_{i} service, a score from the reward model ArmoRM-Llama3-8B-v0.1 (Wang et al., 2024a). Our simulator retains only these quantities and a question identifier; i.e., neither the prompts nor the generated text are used. The data contain 1,319 GSM8K questions and 546 GPQA questions. Since Best-of-nin_{i} service requires the correctness, token, and reward records to be aligned for every included model, we remove one GPQA question that fails this alignment check jointly from all models whenever Best-of-nin_{i} variants are in use, leaving 545 GPQA questions in those experiments; no questions are removed from GSM8K. As a result, every retained model has the same question set and 128 recorded generations per question.

Base models and listed prices.

We use the nine base models listed in Table 2, together with their publicly listed prices. To determine the per-output-token price of each model, we follow the procedure of Velasco et al. (2026a): we refer to the Hugging Face list of inference providers1212 12 https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/index, consulted on December 30, 2025. and, for each model, compute the average output-token price across the listed providers that offer access to that model. More formally, we denote by λm\lambda_{m} the resulting listed price of model mm in USD per 10610^{6} output tokens. Throughout, all monetary quantities are reported in units of 10−610^{-6} USD, so that the numerical value of λm\lambda_{m} coincides with the price per output token in these units.

Provider construction.

To instantiate providers with a cost–quality trade-off, we build each provider from a base model mm and a service multiplicity nin_{i}, and write i=(m,ni)i=(m,n_{i}) to identify the provider by this pair. A base provider, with ni=1n_{i}=1, serves a query with a single generation of model mm, whereas a Best-of-nin_{i} provider generates nin_{i} candidate responses, incurs the generation cost of all nin_{i} candidates, and returns the candidate with the highest recorded reward score. More concretely, for each question, the simulator samples nin_{i} distinct generations uniformly without replacement from the 128 recorded generations of model mm and, if ni>1n_{i}>1, returns the sampled generation with the highest reward score, resolving ties uniformly through the random ordering of the sampled generations. The correctness of the response, which serves as the score r⁡(xt,yt)r(x_{t},y_{t}) of Section 2, is the binary correctness of the returned generation, while the token count used for pricing and cost includes all nin_{i} candidates. We consider three rosters. The full roster contains all nine base models with ni=1n_{i}=1. The ladder roster contains

m∈{Llama-3-8B,Llama-3.2-1B,Qwen2-1.5B,Qwen2.5-7B}m\in\{\texttt{Llama-3-8B},\texttt{Llama-3.2-1B},\texttt{Qwen2-1.5B},\texttt{Qwen2.5-7B}\}

at each multiplicity ni∈{1,2,4}n_{i}\in\{1,2,4\}, for a total of 12 providers. The ladder roster therefore introduces a direct cost–quality trade-off within each base model, in addition to the variation across model families. The strong-competition roster is used on GPQA only and contains the newest large model and the smallest model of each family, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2-0.5B, all with ni=1n_{i}=1.

Empirical quality, price, and cost.

We now specify how the quantities of Section 2 are instantiated from the recorded data. To this end, it is important to distinguish the listed price, the query price, and the generation cost. The listed price λm\lambda_{m} is the public per-token rate in Table 2; it is known before routing and does not depend on the realized output length. We define the realized query price Vi,tV_{i,t} of provider i=(m,ni)i=(m,n_{i}) in step tt as the listed price λm\lambda_{m} times the total number of output tokens across the nin_{i} recorded generations sampled in that step, i.e., the amount a platform using the model at its listed rate would be invoiced once the output lengths are known. Thus, a Best-of-nin_{i} query is billed for every generated candidate, not only for the returned response. Since the data do not contain the providers’ true generation costs, we construct the private realized generation cost as

ci,t≔Vi,t1+μ,μ=0.25,c_{i,t}\coloneqq\frac{V_{i,t}}{1+\mu},\qquad\mu=0.25, (65)

where μ\mu is a (fixed) margin. It is worth noting that the margin μ\mu is used only to construct the latent cost observations, and it is neither supplied to nor used by the platform. Building on the above, the empirical quality qiq_{i} of provider ii is their expected correctness under a uniformly sampled benchmark question and the generation-sampling procedure above. For a base provider, it is the mean correctness over all recorded question–generation pairs, while for a Best-of-nin_{i} provider, it is computed exactly from the empirical joint distribution of reward scores and correctness, including uniform tie-breaking. Analogously, the cost distribution 𝒫ic\mathcal{P}^{c}_{i} of provider ii is the distribution of the realized generation cost ci,tc_{i,t} in Eq. (65) under the same sampling procedure as qiq_{i}, and c¯i\bar{c}_{i} is its mean. Since query price and generation cost are proportional by construction, the mean query price of provider ii is v¯i=(1+μ)​c¯i\bar{v}_{i}=(1+\mu)\bar{c}_{i}. These quantities are used only for evaluation and for constructing perfect-information reference quantities; they are not given to the platform. Finally, in our primary experiments, providers bid their empirical-mean cost estimate c^i,t\hat{c}_{i,t}, i.e., they follow the equilibrium strategy σi∗\sigma_{i}^{*} of Eq. (8), and payments follow the rule of Eq. (5).

Settings and platform parameters.

For each roster and benchmark, we place the quality threshold qminq_{\min} at the midpoint between two adjacent empirical provider qualities. Table 3 reports, for each of the resulting five settings, the exact threshold, the benchmark size KK, the number of empirically qualified providers, and the lowest-cost qualified provider i∗i^{*} of Eq. (10).

We set the confidence level to δ=0.05\delta=0.05. The output-token cap entering the cost bound is fixed at Lmax=512L_{\max}=512, and the cost bound cmaxc_{\max} of Section 2, which also caps every payment, is set to

cmax=Lmax​maxi=(m,ni)​ni​λm,c_{\max}=L_{\max}\max_{i=(m,n_{i})}n_{i}\lambda_{m}, (66)

which gives cmax≈102c_{\max}\approx 102 for the full roster, cmax≈300c_{\max}\approx 300 for the ladder roster and cmax≈75c_{\max}\approx 75 for the strong-competition roster. Since private costs are obtained by deflating query prices by 1+μ1+\mu, this ceiling also bounds every realized provider cost, as required by our model. Interestingly, the two full-roster settings provide qualitatively different tests of routing by listed price. The lowest listed rate belongs to Qwen2.5-3B, which is i∗i^{*} on GSM8K and is qualified but not i∗i^{*} on GPQA. Listed-price routing is therefore, respectively, aligned with and only partially informative about the platform’s target decision.

Episode construction and randomization.

At the beginning of every episode, the benchmark questions are placed in a seeded random permutation. For every step and every provider, the simulator preassigns a potential outcome using the recorded-generation sampling rule above; only the selected provider’s outcome is then revealed, while the potential outcomes of nonselected providers remain unavailable to the platform. This preserves the platform’s information design of Section 2 while allowing different policies to be evaluated on matched potential outcomes. The first NN steps initialize the platform as prescribed in Section 2, selecting every provider exactly once in a seeded random order, and all subsequent steps follow the platform’s selection and payment rules using the pre-step state.

Exploration steps.

In every experiment of this appendix the platform runs with the exploration rule of Eq. (3). At the beginning of step t>Nt>N, if some estimated-qualified provider i∈𝒬^ti\in\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} (Eq. (2)), which we also refer to as an eligible provider, has been selected fewer than

g⁡(t)=k​(t/N)α,k=2,α=3/4,g(t)=k\,(t/N)^{\alpha},\qquad k=2,\;\alpha=3/4,

times, i.e., if 𝒮t≠∅{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\neq\emptyset, the step is an exploration step: one of the under-sampled eligible providers in 𝒮t{\mathcal{S}}_{t} is drawn uniformly at random, serves the query and is paid cmaxc_{\max}; otherwise it is a non-exploration step, selected and paid according to Eqs. (3) and (5). Exploration steps count toward every selection statistic, regret, generation cost, query price and amount paid; the winning bid and the payment on non-exploration steps are reported over those steps only. The routing baselines and the no-quality-filter ablation do not explore.

Routing policies.

Our primary comparison uses three routing policies, none of which observes private generation costs: (i) uniform routing among eligible providers, (ii) lowest-listed-price routing among eligible providers, and (iii) lowest-listed-price routing without quality screening. Policy (i) constructs the same online estimated-qualified set 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} as the platform, i.e., it may use the observed scores, the selection counts, the threshold qminq_{\min}, and the confidence radius β⁡(mi,t)\beta(m_{i,t}) of Eq. (2), and selects uniformly at random from 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}; it uses neither bids nor listed prices, and thus isolates the contribution of cost-sensitive selection after online quality screening. Policy (ii) constructs the same 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t} and then minimizes the public effective listed rate

λ¯i≔ni​λmfor ​i=(m,ni),\bar{\lambda}_{i}\coloneqq n_{i}\lambda_{m}\qquad\text{for }i=(m,n_{i}),

breaking ties uniformly at random; it observes listed rates but neither provider bids nor generation costs, and the realized response length is not known at selection time. Policy (iii) is static: it minimizes λ¯i\bar{\lambda}_{i} over the entire roster, irrespective of observed quality, and requires only the public listed rates. It therefore provides a direct measure of the reliability lost when routing ignores the quality requirement. In addition, we consider a no-quality-filter ablation of the platform, which retains the optimistic bidding index bi,t−cmax​β​(mi,t)b_{i,t}-c_{\max}\,\beta(m_{i,t}) of Eq. (3), the confidence radius β⁡(mi,t)\beta(m_{i,t}), and the critical payment of Eq. (4), but minimizes the index over the full roster rather than over 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}; this ablation isolates the contribution of online quality screening. The platform pays πt\pi_{t} as in Eq. (5), the routing policies pay the query price of the selected provider, and both are reported as the amount paid.

Horizons and long-run evaluation.

To examine longer-run behavior, we additionally run every setting for T=70,000T=70{,}000 queries and 30 independent runs, paired across rules, corresponding to 54 passes over the GSM8K benchmark and 129 passes over GPQA, with the final pass only partially used. At the beginning of each additional pass, the simulator draws a fresh seeded permutation of all benchmark questions and fresh recorded generations for every provider–question pair, so that the same generation may reappear in different passes; extending the horizon leaves the complete first pass unchanged. This resampling procedure approximates repeated draws from each provider’s empirical outcome distribution. It does not create new questions or new model generations, and the resulting long-horizon evidence remains conditional on the observed benchmark and generation pools.

Metrics.

Our main metrics are the quality regret RTqual=∑t=1T(qmin−qIt)+R_{T}^{\mathrm{qual}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}(q_{\min}-q_{I_{t}})^{+} of Theorem 7 and the generation-cost regret RTgen=∑t=1T(c¯It−c¯i∗)+R_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\bar{c}_{I_{t}}-\bar{c}_{i^{*}})^{+} of Theorem 8, reported both cumulatively and per query. Note that both regrets are computed using the empirical provider parameters qiq_{i} and c¯i\bar{c}_{i} rather than the realized correctness labels and costs, which are subject to sampling noise. We report realized accuracy separately as

Acc^T=1T​∑t=1Tr⁡(xt,yt),\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{T}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r(x_{t},y_{t}),

together with the share of unqualified selections,

1T∑t=1T𝟙{It∉𝒬},\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\{I_{t}\notin\mathcal{Q}\},

the selection share of i∗i^{*}, provider-level selection counts, and whether i∗i^{*} is the unique most selected provider. The economic outcomes comprise realized generation cost per query, query price per query, and the amount paid per query under the policy-specific convention above. For the platform and its no-quality-filter ablation, we additionally report the winning standing bid, the total payment on non-exploration steps, the cumulative excess payment ETpay=∑t=1T(πt−c¯(2))+E_{T}^{\mathrm{pay}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\pi_{t}-\bar{c}_{(2)})^{+} bounded in Theorem 9, and the provider payoff ∑t:It=i(πt−ci,t)\sum_{t:I_{t}=i}\bigl(\pi_{t}-c_{i,t}\bigr). Where useful, these quantities are reported both over the full episode and after initialization, since initialization pays cmaxc_{\max} by construction. Payment diagnostics compare the realized payments on non-exploration steps with the upper bound πt≤min⁡{cmax,c¯(2)+cmax​β​(mIt,t)}\pi_{t}\leq\min\{c_{\max},\,\bar{c}_{(2)}+c_{\max}\,\beta(m_{I_{t},t})\} of Lemma 11 and with the lower bound πt≥max⁡{0,c¯It−cmax​β​(mIt,t)}\pi_{t}\geq\max\{0,\,\bar{c}_{I_{t}}-c_{\max}\,\beta(m_{I_{t},t})\}, which holds on ℰ\mathcal{E} because, by Proposition 1, the selected provider bids c^It,t≤PIt,t\hat{c}_{I_{t},t}\leq P_{I_{t},t}. We further report the realized frequency of the good event ℰ\mathcal{E} of Lemma 1 and compare the post-initialization selections of providers i≠i∗i\neq i^{*} with the corresponding bounds MiM_{i} of Lemma 8 for unqualified providers and max⁡{Li,⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1}\max\{L_{i},\,\lceil g(T)\rceil-1\} of Lemma 9 for qualified ones, where LiL_{i} is defined in Lemma 7. Accordingly, when reporting Bid​(T)B_{\mathrm{id}}(T) and TidT_{\mathrm{id}}, we replace the exploration term k​(T/N)αk(T/N)^{\alpha} of Theorem 3 by the cap ⌈g⁡(T)⌉−1<k​(T/N)α\lceil g(T)\rceil-1<k(T/N)^{\alpha} of Lemma 9, which yields a slightly tighter bound that is also valid by the proof of Theorem 3. For the long-horizon experiment, we additionally report the size of the estimated-qualified set 𝒬^t\hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{t}, the probability that i∗i^{*} is the unique most selected provider, and moving-average selection and payment statistics with window size KK.

Aggregation and uncertainty.

Episode-level tables report the mean and standard deviation across runs. For one-pass figures, points and selection shares are shown with normal-approximation 95% intervals, x¯±1.96​sx/R\overline{x}\pm 1.96\,s_{x}/\sqrt{R}, where RR is the number of runs and sxs_{x} is their sample standard deviation. Long-horizon trajectory figures use the pointwise median across runs as the central trajectory and the empirical 10th–90th percentile range as a band. Long-horizon checkpoint tables report means across runs, while identification probabilities are the corresponding empirical fractions of runs.
